title: Air conditioning isn't enough to cool hot New Orleans homes - Verite News
description:
The house’s central air conditioning couldn’t keep up.
As summer days and nights grow warmer, it’s harder for New Orleans residents like Sutton to keep their home cool with the cost of energy.
Air conditioning or medication?
Parker said she blasts her window air conditioning unit in the bedroom, turning it to 72 degrees.
The choice between running the air conditioning and affording medications can be deadly, Reed said.
text:
Yana Sutton grew up between Hollygrove and Gert Town, and now, she spends nearly every day there to take care of her grandmother. But it was only in the past few years that Sutton realized how much the extreme heat in the neighborhood was taking a toll on her grandmother’s health.

“The heat is heaviest in the bedroom,” which is in the back of the Gert Town house, Sutton said. The neighborhood has far more concrete and buildings than trees than other parts of the city. The imbalanced landscape amplifies the amount of heat and humidity that passes into her grandmother’s house from a back room. The house’s central air conditioning couldn’t keep up.

Her grandmother thought she was resting, but her doctors said the high temperatures actually raised her blood pressure and exacerbated her pre-diabetes. Her grandmother also slept far longer than she intended.

“She says she’d wake up soaking wet,” Sutton said. “(The doctor) said when you get up in age, if your blood pressure is fluctuating and you’re in this tremendous amount of heat, your brain and everything is not signaling you to wake up.”

Sutton has since blocked the room to the limit the outside air seeping into the rest of the house, helping to keep her grandmother’s bedroom cool.

“ We see the difference because her blood pressure now is stable,” Sutton said.

As summer days and nights grow warmer, it’s harder for New Orleans residents like Sutton to keep their home cool with the cost of energy. That’s especially true when they live in the city’s concrete-laden hotspots like Gert Town, Hollygrove and areas in the Upper Ninth Ward.

“ Hollygrove is like a dome in a sense, where it’s trapping the heat,” she said.

A study published in the Journal of Urban Health in June found that even when New Orleans residents had air conditioning units, they struggled to keep the temperature in their homes under 80 degrees overnight.

Researchers from RAND and Johns Hopkins University collaborated with the team at iSeeChange, a crowd-sourced platform for reporting climate and weather observations, to track the temperature inside the bedrooms of 114 New Orleans residents during the summers of 2023 and 2024. The residents were recruited from five neighborhoods: Hollygrove, Dixon, Desire, Florida and Bunny Friend.

Past research had indicated that the neighborhoods suffered from worse heat than other parts of the city, amplified by the urban heat island effect. Sutton said it affects everything from seniors’ health to the integrity of their houses.

The Hollygrove-Dixon Neighborhood Association partnered with CAPA Strategies and the Center for Collaborative Heat Monitoring to map the how temperatures changed throughout the day on July 25, 2025 across New Orleans. This map shows the temperatures recorded in the afternoon between 3 p.m. and 4 p.m. Other map layers show the temperatures recorded in the morning and evening. (Credit: CAPA Strategies and the Center for Collaborative Heat Monitoring)

Hollygrove resident Deanna Simon helped map heat across the city on a single July day in 2025 during a study by the Hollygrove-Dixon Neighborhood Association. The temperature snapshot showed heat disparities across the city based on tree canopy, the concentration of impervious surfaces and proximity to the lake. It also recorded the hottest temperatures between 7 p.m. and 8 p.m.

“The heat kind of lingers for a long time. It has to be middle morning before you start feeling really cool,” Simon said, until the area reabsorbs the heat.

Several peer-reviewed studies have linked higher temperatures to worse sleep, which can place more stress on the body. Warm nights can be especially dangerous for people with chronic conditions, people over 65, low-income communities, communities of color and women. The heat can increase the risk of various heart problems, such as strokes or heart disease, and even lead to death.

By the end of the century, some researchers estimate that the risk of death from excessively hot nights will be six times more likely as a result of global warming, predominantly caused by humans burning fossil fuels.

New Orleans’ “unique heat risk”

RAND’s Lena Easton-Calabria, a co-author of the new study, said they chose to focus on New Orleans because it’s seeing some of the “most severe heat trends,” and high poverty rate.

“These are things that … come together and create a very unique heat risk and make the population very vulnerable,” Easton-Calabria said.

An analysis by the policy-neutral nonprofit Climate Central found that the average temperature in New Orleans, during the day and at night, has warmed by more than 4 degrees from June through August since 1970. The nonprofit also estimated that New Orleans residents lost an average of 61 hours of sleep per year from 2020 to 2025, in part due to climate change.

Not surprisingly, the June indoor heat study found that the hotter it is outside, the hotter temperatures can be indoors. But in a state like Louisiana, which has some of the highest energy costs in the country, the use of air conditioning varied in response to the temperatures and affected how cool the study’s participants could keep their homes.

Public health recommendations for sleeping temperatures can vary. One study in Boston found their participants slept best between 68 degrees and 77 degrees. Most cities that have passed cooling standards so far have required landlords to ensure their properties can remain under about 80 degrees, including New Orleans’ Healthy Homes Ordinance.

But even cooling the bedroom to 80 degrees can be challenging, according to the recent study. Unless participants had central air conditioning and reported that they ran the system most or all of the time, temperatures in the bedroom were expected to exceed 80 degrees if it was hotter than 90 degrees during the day. During the study, at least one bedroom heated up to 101 degrees overnight, while others maxed out at 65 degrees.

Most of the study’s participants were Black and made less than $50,000 a year, including the homeowners. Study co-author Jaime Madrigano, a public health professor at Johns Hopkins, said while most cooling standards attempt to protect renters, their findings suggest low-income homeowners also need help with staying cool.

Homeowners made up most of the study and more than half made less than the city’s median household income. At least in the recent study, the homeowners were more likely to report using their air conditioner only half of the time or rarely.

Air conditioning or medication?

In Hollygrove, Dorethea Parker saw herself in the study’s findings. She’s owned her house for about 35 years. Parker said she blasts her window air conditioning unit in the bedroom, turning it to 72 degrees. Even still, cooling her bedroom at night is often a losing battle against the city’s steamy summer heat.

“It’s extremely hot in my house,” she said. “I definitely wake up some nights because of the heat.”

She typically keeps the rest of her window units off to save on her energy bill. Part of Parker’s problem is that her walls aren’t well-insulated. Plus, she believes the cool air escapes beneath the floorboards of her elevated home.

Caroline Reed, another study co-author who worked with iSeeChange at the time, said while several studies, including this one, have shown that air conditioning is a life-saving tool during extreme heat, their study suggests that air conditioning alone won’t solve the problem.

Reed focused on outreach to residents and placing the temperature sensors in their homes. She said she often heard residents, especially those with ongoing health problems, talk about how difficult and expensive it was to cool their homes. People who ran their air conditioning all the time, to keep up with the heat, typically reported spending at least $200 more on their energy bills than those who saved on energy but had hotter houses.

Reed said some residents who limited their energy use or had window units that may have been less efficient at cooling couldn’t find relief from the heat outside when they came inside. Dealing with the persistent heat would add stress to their bodies and their finances.

“I think that, unfortunately, air conditioning, while it’s incredibly essential, still will always not be able to compete with other essentials in terms of your water bill, your food, or your medications,” Reed said.

The choice between running the air conditioning and affording medications can be deadly, Reed said.

“We know that exposure to extreme heat over short or long amounts of time is just really dangerous for folks,” she said. “When people are hospitalized, or in the worst case scenario, … even die from extreme heat, a lot of times they’re found in their homes.”

Investing in cooling

The researchers and iSeeChange team said they hope studies like this can help inform heat policies at all levels of government.

In New Orleans, Easton-Calabria and Madrigano said setting a cooling standard for renters establishes the concept of cooling — or maintaining a healthy temperature — as a right.

“It’s a good first step,” Madrigano said. But questions remain about how to implement and enforce the standard, and more would need to be done to ensure affordability doesn’t present a barrier.

“I think it is evident, from our research and others, that the cost of running AC needs to be accounted for when policymakers are trying to protect their constituents during extreme weather,” Madrigano said. “Access, alone, should not be the only consideration, and energy assistance programs are going to be crucial to saving lives.”

Currently, programs to help reduce the cost of energy bills, either as financial assistance or through energy efficiency, are limited.

The federal Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program is the primary source for public assistance with energy bills, but can only serve a limited number of residents. From April to September 2024, about 80,000 Louisianians received $200 to $800 to offset cooling costs. The Trump administration and U.S. House of Representatives have proposed cutting the program entirely next year, though a similar proposal in 2025 wasn’t enacted by Congress as the program has bipartisan support.

Housing advocacy groups in New Orleans have pushed for more funding toward programs to upgrade houses to seal them against the weather, also known as weatherizing.

This can include sealing the cracks in a building with foam to prevent from air leaking inside. Material known as weather-stripping can similarly be used for gaps around windows and doors to block drafts. Contractors can also install more insulation or repair holes in a house’s heating and cooling system.

But homeowners only have access to two programs: the federal Weatherization Assistance Program and Entergy New Orleans’ EnergySmart program.

Parker, who lives in Hollygrove, said the EnergySmart program had its limits. While her free home assessment was helpful, the company only installs insulation in the attic, not the walls or the floors.

Beau Tidwell, a spokesperson for Entergy New Orleans, said the company recommends for residents with needs beyond the scope of EntergySmart to apply for Weatherization Assistance Program. The federal program will install wall insulation, he said, and Quad Area Weatherization can help with applications. Though, the federal program often has a long waitlist and limited funding.

The latest proposal for addressing housing needs in New Orleans — created through a process called HousingNOLA — called for the city to invest about $3 million to weatherize and equip homes with solar panels and batteries to reduce residents’ energy burden, on top of improving the housing stock.

Reed said she believes dedicating more government resources to limiting extreme heat will be the main area for growth, as well as preventative care from healthcare providers.

“ Extreme heat is still a relatively emerging area,” Reed said. “People are trying to better understand the ways that it presents risks to our communities and what solutions are actually offerable, and then within those solutions, what’s actually affordable.”

Volunteers with the Hollygrove-Dixon Neighborhood Association plan to advocate for more tree plantings and other ways to reduce the heat island effect, possibly making it easier for cooling systems to keep up.

This study was the first in a series of publications looking at the effects of extreme heat in New Orleans. iSeeChange has also launched a new campaign inviting residents to share their experiences with heat.

Sutton said the neighborhood association also plans to present a proposal to the New Orleans City Council early next year using the research and community input to request more resources to address heat.

title: Battery material recycling plant outside Atlanta to restart under new owners - AJC.com
description:

title: India's Lithium Battery Manufacturing Sector to Create 3 Million Jobs by 2030, says Adecco India
description:
The sector is projected to generate 1.5 to 2 million jobs, 25% direct and 75% indirect, by 2030.
According to Deepesh Gupta, Director and Head of General Staffing, Adecco India, “India’s battery manufacturing journey is no longer just a policy ambition; it is now translating into plant-level capacity.
Battery Recycling and Circular Economy Manufacturing is emerging as one of the sector’s fastest-growing talent segments as end-of-life volumes begin to build.
“Despite the pace of capacity announcements, specialised battery talent availability continues to lag industry demand by 25-30% across electrochemistry, materials science, battery process engineering and functional safety.
With deep expertise in engineering, manufacturing and specialised workforce solutions, Adecco India is well positioned to support companies in building this future-ready talent base.
text:
Cell manufacturing, battery components and recycling emerge as the fastest-growing talent engines, with 30-35% rise in demand for specialised battery engineering roles

Mumbai, 8th September 2026: India is transforming from importing and assembling lithium-ion cells to building a domestic cell-to-pack manufacturing base. The country’s battery industry is entering its most capital-intensive and employment-intensive phase, evolving from an assembly and import-dependent opportunity into a fully integrated cell-to-recycling industrial ecosystem, according to Adecco India. The sector is projected to generate 1.5 to 2 million jobs, 25% direct and 75% indirect, by 2030. Hiring is expected to grow by 25% to 30% Y-o-Y, with the next decade defined less by conventional assembly-line roles and more by specialised electrochemistry, materials science and battery process engineering capabilities across the value chain.

According to Deepesh Gupta, Director and Head of General Staffing, Adecco India, “India’s battery manufacturing journey is no longer just a policy ambition; it is now translating into plant-level capacity. Under the PLI Scheme for Advanced Chemistry Cells, the Government of India has committed Rs. 18,100 crore to develop 50 GWh of domestic ACC manufacturing capacity, with an additional 5 GWh reserved for niche chemistries. A new component manufacturing incentive scheme of nearly Rs. 12,000 crore is also under consideration for cathode and anode active materials, copper foil, electrolytes and separators. With battery manufacturing capacity currently at around 60 GWh and expected to approach 100 GWh by the end of 2026, along with upcoming gigafactory investments in Gujarat, Karnataka, Haryana and Telangana, the sector is moving beyond assembly and building the depth of a full industrial ecosystem. Since battery components account for more than 60% of cell cost, and India continues to depend heavily on imported lithium, cobalt and refined battery-grade materials, workforce planning must cover the entire value chain, from cell chemistry and pack integration to end-of-life recycling, not just finished-vehicle manufacturing,”

“Catalysing the vision of ‘Atmanirbhar Bharat’, this localisation drive, supported by the Critical Minerals Mission and India’s participation in the Quad Critical Minerals Initiative Framework, will reduce India’s reliance on imported cells and refined materials, strengthen energy security, and support the Net-Zero target by 2070, while creating employment opportunities across both established manufacturing hubs and emerging Tier-2 and Tier-3 industrial corridors,” he added.

Top specialised roles Hiring growth (FY26 vs FY27) Pay Range (7+ years) Average compensation growth (FY26 vs FY27) Cell Chemistry & Materials Engineer 25-30% ₹28-55 LPA 15%-20% Battery Management System (BMS) Engineer 30-35% ₹22-45 LPA 18-25% Gigafactory Process & Manufacturing Engineer 35-40% ₹18-35 LPA 12-18% Battery Testing, Safety & Quality Engineer 25-30% ₹20-38 LPA 15-20% Battery Recycling & Circular Economy Specialist 30-40% ₹22-45 LPA 20-30%

Lithium Battery manufacturing is expected to contribute 50% – 60% of India’s projected green manufacturing jobs by 2030, with specialised battery engineering talent commanding salary premiums of up to 35% to 40% over conventional manufacturing and electronics roles.

Gigafactory clusters continue to be the primary employment engine for the sector, concentrated in Karnataka, Telangana, Gujarat and Haryana, with individual facility capacities ranging from 6 GWh to upwards of 16 GWh of cell and pack manufacturing capacity. 70% of total hiring demand is concentrated across these clusters, with 30% of new mandates expected to originate from Tier-2 and Tier-3 industrial corridors as component parks, battery recycling facilities and supplier ecosystems mature around the anchor gigafactories. State-wise, karnataka and Gujarat are expected to account for the largest share of this hiring at 24% and 22% respectively, followed by Telangana (18%) and Haryana (14%), as cell manufacturing, pack assembly and ancillary supplier capacity scales across these clusters.

The Cell Manufacturing and Battery Components segment will account for the largest share of hiring (42%-45%), extending well beyond gigafactory operators into cathode and anode active material producers, copper foil, electrolyte and separator manufacturers, and precursor chemical suppliers, as India works to localise a supply chain. Currently, China controls roughly 80% of global copper foil output and refines the majority of the world’s lithium, nickel and cobalt.

Talent planning is also beginning to look beyond lithium-ion chemistry. A 2026 CEEW assessment argues that India will need to diversify its battery chemistries as demand could reach around 1.3 TWh annually by 2047, with sodium-ion batteries emerging as a credible pathway to supporting the country’s energy transition and reducing supply-chain vulnerabilities. Several key sodium-ion battery components, including cathode materials, hard-carbon anodes, electrolytes and aluminium current collectors, can draw on India’s existing industrial capabilities in pharmaceuticals, fertilisers, textiles and chemicals, potentially enabling significant domestic value addition and opening a parallel talent pathway for chemical and process engineers already embedded in these sectors. Emerging players commercialising hard carbon made from agricultural and bio waste for sodium-ion batteries with support from the Department of Science and Technology and the Technology Development Board, point to the kind of cross-sector talent movement this diversification could unlock.

Entry-level demand is strongest across process engineering, cell testing, validation and quality functions (45%), while mid-level hiring is increasingly concentrated on Battery Management System Engineers, Process and Automation Engineers, and Materials and Electrochemistry Engineers (40%). At the senior level, demand centres on Cell Chemistry Scientists, Functional Safety Leaders and Advanced Manufacturing Heads (15%).

Battery Recycling and Circular Economy Manufacturing is emerging as one of the sector’s fastest-growing talent segments as end-of-life volumes begin to build. With India currently recycling only a small fraction of its end-of-life lithium-ion batteries, and industry estimates pointing to a recycling market opportunity of around USD 3.5 billion by 2030, alongside the Government’s Critical Minerals Mission and the KABIL joint venture working to secure upstream lithium, cobalt and nickel supply, recycling and materials recovery are becoming central to the sector’s workforce planning rather than a peripheral function. Hiring in this segment is projected to grow by 25-30%, with demand shifting towards Hydrometallurgy Engineers, Battery Diagnostics Specialists and EPR Compliance Leaders, and salary premiums of up to 30%-40% reflecting an acute skill shortage estimated at 45%.

“Despite the pace of capacity announcements, specialised battery talent availability continues to lag industry demand by 25-30% across electrochemistry, materials science, battery process engineering and functional safety. A significant share of India’s conventional electronics and automotive manufacturing workforce, skilled in mechanical and electrical assembly, is not directly transferable to gigafactory environments without structured reskilling in cell chemistry, cleanroom protocols and battery safety systems. Addressing this gap will require accelerated reskilling of the existing manufacturing workforce, deeper industry-academia collaboration with chemical engineering and materials science institutions, and sustained investment in specialised battery technical education,” Deepesh added.

Looking ahead, organisations that build layered, function-specific talent pipelines, spanning cell chemistry, process manufacturing, functional safety and materials recovery, will be best placed to lead India’s battery manufacturing ecosystem as it scales. A one-size-fits-all workforce strategy will not work for a manufacturing base this technically complex and still this early in its build-out. With deep expertise in engineering, manufacturing and specialised workforce solutions, Adecco India is well positioned to support companies in building this future-ready talent base.

title: Lexus NX Drops Gas-Only Power for 2027 - WJBF
authors: Robert R. Guio, TestMiles.com, Robert R. Guio, TestMiles.com
description:
(TestMiles) – The 2027 Lexus NX drops its gas-only choices, expands plug-in capability and adds new safety, chassis and cabin technology for luxury SUV buyers.
It is how much these changes will cost when the 2027 NX reaches showrooms.
For 2027, Lexus is narrowing that decision to two powertrain families: the NX 350h hybrid and NX 450h+ plug-in hybrid.
For 2027, Lexus is also making DC fast-charging capability standard on NX plug-in hybrid grades.
Chassis Changes Aim Beyond Efficiency Lexus is not presenting the 2027 NX as merely a powertrain update.
text:
(TestMiles) – The 2027 Lexus NX drops its gas-only choices, expands plug-in capability and adds new safety, chassis and cabin technology for luxury SUV buyers.

Lexus is making one of its most consequential changes to the NX since the compact luxury crossover arrived in 2014. For the 2027 model year, the NX will no longer offer a conventional gasoline-only powertrain. Every version will be either a hybrid or a plug-in hybrid.

That does not mean the NX has become an all-electric vehicle. Lexus uses the term “100% electrified” because every powertrain in the lineup will use an electric motor and battery, but both the NX 350h hybrid and NX 450h+ plug-in hybrid still use gasoline engines. The distinction matters because shoppers will not need to depend on public charging to own the new NX, even though one version can be plugged in.

The change arrives as Lexus gives the NX a broader update that reaches well beyond the engine bay. The company says the 2027 model receives a redesigned hybrid system, a larger-capacity plug-in battery, standard DC fast charging on PHEV grades, stronger body structure, revised steering and suspension tuning, a standard 14-inch infotainment display, Lexus Safety System+ 4.0 and an unusual new cabin feature called Sensory Concierge.

Pricing and final U.S. fuel-economy ratings have not yet been announced, so the most important question for buyers is not simply what Lexus has added. It is how much these changes will cost when the 2027 NX reaches showrooms.

The NX Ends Its Gas-Only Era

The outgoing NX lineup gave buyers several ways into the model, including a turbocharged gasoline version as well as hybrid and plug-in hybrid choices. For 2027, Lexus is narrowing that decision to two powertrain families: the NX 350h hybrid and NX 450h+ plug-in hybrid.

That makes the NX a useful example of how electrification is spreading through the market without requiring every buyer to move directly into a battery-electric vehicle. A conventional hybrid charges its traction battery through the engine and regenerative braking. A plug-in hybrid carries a larger battery that can be charged from an external source and can cover part of a trip on electric power before operating more like a conventional hybrid.

Lexus says the new hybrid hardware uses an e-Axle that combines the transaxle, electric motor and power control unit into a more compact assembly. The inverter also adopts silicon-carbide power semiconductors, a change Lexus says contributes to further efficiency gains.

The company says it has also changed how electric power is delivered during acceleration. More battery assistance is intended to reduce the familiar hybrid effect in which engine speed rises more quickly than vehicle speed. Lexus describes the goal as a more linear relationship between what the driver asks for with the accelerator and what the vehicle delivers.

All-wheel-drive versions also receive revised E-Four control. Instead of using the rear electric motor only in selected circumstances such as launch, cornering or wheel slip, Lexus says the system can maintain all-wheel-drive operation during straight-line driving as well. The intended benefit is a steadier sense of traction and greater stability on low-grip roads.

A Bigger Bet on Plug-In Power

The NX 450h+ receives the most significant hardware change. Lexus says its newly developed lithium-ion battery provides 30 percent more capacity and 8 percent more output than before. The company has not yet published final EPA electric-range ratings for the 2027 model, so the size of the real-world improvement remains to be independently established.

That matters because a plug-in hybrid becomes more useful when its electric capability can cover a meaningful share of ordinary commuting and errands. A driver who can recharge at home may be able to complete many short trips without starting the gasoline engine. On a longer journey, the vehicle can continue using its gasoline-electric hybrid system after the charge is depleted.

For 2027, Lexus is also making DC fast-charging capability standard on NX plug-in hybrid grades. That could make the NX 450h+ easier to replenish during a road trip or a busy day away from home, but the usefulness will depend on charging performance that Lexus has not yet detailed.

There are important numbers still missing. Lexus has not yet published the NX 450h+ peak DC charging rate, a 10-to-80-percent charging time, final battery capacity in kilowatt-hours, final EPA electric range or final combined efficiency. Those figures will determine whether DC charging is a genuinely useful everyday feature or primarily an added convenience.

The battery’s physical placement is also part of the chassis story. Lexus says it changed the cell layout from longitudinal to transverse, mounted the battery lower and used the new arrangement to increase lateral rigidity. In other words, the larger battery is being asked to do more than store electricity; its packaging is also being used as part of the vehicle’s structural strategy.

Chassis Changes Aim Beyond Efficiency

Lexus is not presenting the 2027 NX as merely a powertrain update. Engineers reinforced the front and rear portions of the body, added a floor cross member, strengthened the tunnel area and redesigned the suspension towers with integrated structural components.

Those changes are intended to improve more than cornering. A stiffer body gives suspension components a more consistent platform from which to work, and Lexus says the result should include sharper handling, less road noise and improved ride comfort.

On models without Adaptive Variable Suspension, new shock absorbers use ultra-low-speed valves designed to react to very small suspension movements. Lexus says the goal is to keep the body flatter over road undulations without making the ride harsh. The company tuned the NX at Toyota Technical Center Shimoyama in Japan and at Germany’s Nürburgring.

The steering system also changes. The wheel itself is 0.4 inch smaller in diameter, measuring 14.2 inches, while a variable-ratio steering rack and retuned electric power steering are intended to improve maneuverability and feedback. The accelerator pedal assembly has been revised to reduce friction, and a new brake-control function can apply subtle braking during cornering to help manage yaw and roll during abrupt maneuvers.

Lexus also says it used large-scale driving-position data to revise seat and steering-wheel relationships, including a wider telescoping adjustment range. These are the sorts of changes that rarely dominate a launch headline, but they can matter every time a driver climbs into the vehicle.

Luxury Moves Into the Senses

The exterior update keeps the basic NX silhouette while revising lighting, trim and aerodynamic details. The front integrates lighting and functional elements more closely into the grille, while the rear introduces what Lexus calls its first Double L Signature taillamp treatment. Nine exterior colors are planned, including the new Shaded Ivy and an Incognito finish for F SPORT grades.

Inside, a 12.3-inch digital instrument display sits alongside a 14-inch Lexus Interface touchscreen that is now standard across the lineup. The updated multimedia system adds functions including split-screen viewing and an integrated Drive Recorder that uses exterior cameras to save clips associated with manual or triggered events.

The most unusual option is Sensory Concierge, available on Luxury and F SPORT grades. It coordinates ambient lighting, music, climate settings, seat temperature and fragrance. Three programs—Inspire, Radiance and Revitalize—are intended to create different moods, and occupants can also select fragrances separately.

Lexus has named the scents Shinmei, Seiyo and Hanya, with citrus, floral and musk themes. Whether buyers see that as a thoughtful extension of luxury or a feature they try once and forget will depend heavily on personal taste. It does, however, show where Lexus believes luxury can expand when larger screens and premium audio systems are no longer unusual.

The 2027 NX also moves to Lexus Safety System+ 4.0 as standard equipment. The suite includes pre-collision assistance with pedestrian detection, lane tracing, lane-departure support, radar cruise control, road-sign recognition and Proactive Driving Assist. Additional available features include Traffic Jam Assist, Lane Change Assist, rear pedestrian detection and Front Cross-Traffic Alert.

Traffic Jam Assist can provide temporary hands-free steering support under specified low-speed conditions on limited-access roads, but Lexus still requires the driver to remain attentive and ready to take control. That distinction is important: these are driver-assistance systems, not a promise that the NX can drive itself.

What Buyers Still Need to Know

Lexus plans four grades for 2027: Premium, Premium+, F SPORT and Luxury. With the NX 350h hybrid powertrain, Premium and Premium+ can be ordered with front-wheel drive or all-wheel drive. F SPORT and Luxury hybrids are planned as all-wheel drive only. Every NX 450h+ plug-in hybrid will use all-wheel drive.

That structure simplifies the showroom decision, but it also removes one kind of buyer from the old equation: someone who specifically wanted the response and character of a conventional gasoline turbo engine without hybrid hardware. For everyone else, the choice becomes more straightforward. The NX 350h is the no-plug solution, while the NX 450h+ asks buyers to pay for a larger battery and charging capability in exchange for meaningful electric driving.

The missing pricing will determine how persuasive that trade becomes. Lexus has not yet announced 2027 MSRPs, final grade equipment, final EPA fuel economy, final system horsepower or detailed DC fast-charging performance. Those are not minor footnotes. They are the numbers that will tell buyers whether the plug-in model has moved from an expensive niche choice to the most compelling version of the NX.

The broader point is easier to see. Lexus is not asking NX customers to leap directly from gasoline to a full EV. It is removing the gas-only step and making electrification unavoidable while preserving the long-distance familiarity of a gasoline engine. That is a significant shift for one of the brand’s core crossovers, but it is also a carefully managed one.

For shoppers, the 2027 NX is therefore less about an electric revolution than a new default. Hybrid technology becomes the baseline, plug-in capability becomes the upgrade path, and conventional gasoline-only power leaves the menu. Whether that feels like progress will depend on price, efficiency and how well the new hardware performs when independent testing begins.

title: India's battery boom: 2 million jobs by 2030 as factories, recycling and EV demand reshape work
description:
India’s battery industry is entering a transformative phase where employment creation is becoming as significant as production capacity.
This growth reflects a structural shift from importing and assembling lithium-ion cells to building a complete domestic ecosystem that covers cell manufacturing, pack assembly, component supply and recycling.
Current battery manufacturing capacity stands near 60 GWh and is likely to approach 100 GWh by end-2026, setting the stage for deeper value-chain development beyond simple assembly.
While the battery sector itself is expected to contribute 50–60 per cent of India’s projected green manufacturing jobs by 2030, the wider EV ecosystem could generate 30–40 million jobs, with battery manufacturing, power electronics and automotive software among the fastest-growing talent segments.
The momentum in battery manufacturing is not isolated; it is part of a larger push toward green industrialisation that ties together energy security, climate goals and job creation.
text:
India’s battery industry is entering a transformative phase where employment creation is becoming as significant as production capacity. According to talent solutions firm Adecco India, the sector is projected to generate between 1.5 and 2 million jobs by fiscal year 2029–30.

This growth reflects a structural shift from importing and assembling lithium-ion cells to building a complete domestic ecosystem that covers cell manufacturing, pack assembly, component supply and recycling. The change is not just about making more batteries; it is about creating an industrial base that can support electric mobility, grid storage and clean energy goals while offering diverse career paths.

The employment picture is broadly split into direct and indirect roles, with around one-quarter expected to be direct jobs in factories, engineering and operations, and the remaining three-quarters coming from indirect opportunities in supply chains, logistics, services and ancillary industries.

Hiring in the battery space is anticipated to grow at 25–30 per cent annually over the next few years, driven by rising demand for electric vehicles, government incentives for domestic manufacturing and large-scale investments in gigafactories across states like Gujarat, Karnataka, Haryana and Telangana.

Current battery manufacturing capacity stands near 60 GWh and is likely to approach 100 GWh by end-2026, setting the stage for deeper value-chain development beyond simple assembly.

Cell manufacturing and battery components are likely to account for the largest share of new hiring, roughly 42–45 per cent, as companies move from importing cells to producing them locally. This shift demands specialised skills in electrochemistry, materials science, process engineering and quality control, moving the workforce profile away from conventional assembly-line roles toward more technical positions.

At the same time, battery recycling and circular economy activities are emerging as fast-growing segments, with end-of-life battery volumes expected to rise sharply by 2030. Recycling-related hiring is projected to grow at 25–30 per cent, creating demand for hydrometallurgy engineers, battery diagnostics specialists and compliance experts who can manage environmental norms and extended producer responsibility.

Infrastructure expansion is another major employment driver. As charging networks, battery-swapping stations, grid integration projects and energy corridors scale up, the need for electrical engineers, charging infrastructure specialists and energy network architects is rising.

While the battery sector itself is expected to contribute 50–60 per cent of India’s projected green manufacturing jobs by 2030, the wider EV ecosystem could generate 30–40 million jobs, with battery manufacturing, power electronics and automotive software among the fastest-growing talent segments.

Salary premiums of 35–40 per cent over conventional manufacturing roles are already visible for specialised battery engineers, reflecting the scarcity of skilled talent and the strategic importance of this sector.

The story also connects to broader economic trends. Just as India has begun exporting refined petroleum products to markets like Kenya, Russia and more recently diesel to Europe, the battery industry represents the next frontier where domestic capability can translate into global competitiveness. Local cell production reduces import dependence, strengthens supply chains and positions India as a potential export hub for batteries and related components.

With industry estimates pointing to domestic lithium-ion cell demand reaching around 130 GWh by 2030, of which nearly 100 GWh may come from electric vehicles, the scale of opportunity is substantial. Companies like Exide Industries are already committing significant capital to set up lithium-ion cell plants, with production expected to begin in the near term, signalling confidence in long-term demand.

For job seekers, the implications are clear. Entry-level opportunities are strongest in manufacturing engineering, testing, validation and quality functions, while mid-level demand is rising for battery management system engineers, embedded software developers, power electronics and thermal engineers.

Senior roles are centred on R&D scientists, cell chemistry specialists and advanced manufacturing leaders who can drive innovation and scale. As gigafactory clusters develop in key states, these regions are likely to become primary employment engines, each facility ranging from 6 GWh to over 16 GWh in capacity.

The transition also means that skilling and reskilling will be critical, with training programmes needing to align with industry requirements in electrochemistry, automation, safety standards and sustainability practices.

The momentum in battery manufacturing is not isolated; it is part of a larger push toward green industrialisation that ties together energy security, climate goals and job creation.

With policy support, private investment and rising EV adoption, the battery sector is poised to become one of the most dynamic employment generators in India’s economy over the next decade.

The shift from assembly to full-scale domestic production marks a turning point where India is not just consuming technology but building it, creating opportunities that extend far beyond factory gates into research, design, services and global markets.

SOUTHFIELD, Mich. (WXYZ) — Michigan is moving forward with a pilot program to study a mileage-based road tax as rising numbers of electric and fuel-efficient vehicles cut into the state's gas tax revenue.

Lawmakers earmarked more than $7 million last year to evaluate the option, and a six-month pilot program with 1,000 participants is set to begin in February.

Watch the video report below:

Michigan explores mileage-based road tax with 2027 pilot program

For roughly 100 years, Michigan has funded its roads through a tax collected at the gas pump. But as more drivers make the switch to electric vehicles, that revenue stream is shrinking. Michigan is among many states across the country exploring this option, and some have already implemented it.

Among the questions researchers plan to study is how mileage would be reported to the state. Options range from periodic odometer readings to a smartphone app to GPS systems installed in vehicles — a prospect that drew concern from drivers.

"I'm a little uncomfortable about that personally," driver Michael Sands said.

Spencer Dickhudt, another Michigan driver, said he would prefer to self-report his mileage.

"I would probably prefer to input it myself just because of the whole data thing. It would be nice for people not to see everywhere that I've been," Dickhudt said.

Barry Brown, a Michigan driver who expressed skepticism about the concept, echoed those concerns.

"They need to find another way, especially not GPS tracking, I'm tracked enough already," Brown said.

Dickhudt said he sees the logic behind a mileage-based approach.

"It seems like a fair way to make sure that everyone that uses the roads is paying for them to help keep them maintained and in shape," Dickhudt said.

He also raised a question about how out-of-state drivers would be taxed under such a system.

"We have a lot of tourists who come to Michigan, like from other Midwest states... how are we going to get the tax for them using the roads if their cars aren't registered here," Dickhudt said.

The shift to a mileage-based tax would still likely be years away. In the months ahead, officials plan to conduct more public outreach and education. An advisory committee meets monthly, with the next meeting scheduled for Sept. 28.

title: China halts approvals for new battery energy storage projects amid market slowdown
description:
China has built a large battery-manufacturing ecosystem, particularly around electric vehicles and energy storage.
Caixin reported that in the first half of 2026, China added 21.8GW, or 58.6GWh, of newly commissioned new-type energy storage.
The shift shows the growing role of dedicated storage projects after China ended a rule requiring renewable-energy projects to pair generation with storage.
Policy shifts are reshaping demand The slowdown also follows a policy change that altered how demand for energy storage is generated.
Several provinces, including Gansu, Jilin, Shaanxi, Xinjiang, Hubei, Ningxia, and Qinghai, also introduced compensation policies for storage projects.
text:
Chinese authorities are pausing new greenfield battery-storage project approvals pending capacity review.

Existing factories and approved projects may continue, while market demand slows and prices fall.

Policy shifts and international restrictions are reshaping the sector's growth and supply chain dynamics.

China has temporarily paused approvals for some new battery-cell factory projects aimed at the energy-storage market. Several media outlets report that authorities are reviewing existing and planned capacity, while projects that have not yet broken ground are being held up for now.

The move does not appear to affect every project in the same way. Reuters and ESS News reported that factories already under construction can continue, whereas projects that have not yet broken ground are paused. ESS News also said it found no formally published government decree, National Development and Reform Commission circular, or Ministry of Industry and Information Technology gazette notice, suggesting an administrative pause rather than a formally announced nationwide ban.

China has built a large battery-manufacturing ecosystem, particularly around electric vehicles and energy storage. In recent years, battery suppliers have increasingly viewed grid storage as a major growth sector. Still, the latest reports suggest that authorities are becoming more cautious about approving additional capacity while they assess what is already operational, under construction, or planned.

A cooling market and a growing factory fleet

The pause comes amid a slowdown in the market expected to absorb much of the new manufacturing capacity.

Caixin reported that in the first half of 2026, China added 21.8GW, or 58.6GWh, of newly commissioned new-type energy storage. The power-capacity figure was down 18 percent from a year earlier, while the energy-capacity figure fell 16 percent, according to the reporting cited in the original coverage. The number of new projects was cut in half, even as the average size of projects increased.

Standalone storage accounted for 15.1GW, or 69.3 percent of new installations, according to Caixin. The shift shows the growing role of dedicated storage projects after China ended a rule requiring renewable-energy projects to pair generation with storage. But the slowdown creates challenges for manufacturers that continued announcing facilities while expecting demand to grow rapidly.

The figures help explain why officials may be reassessing the sector’s capacity balance. Even if the overall market continues expanding, factory construction can outpace project deployment. Excess capacity can intensify competition for customers and push prices lower.

The key question for battery makers is therefore not only whether China will continue adding storage capacity, but also how quickly installations will grow and whether existing projects can generate sufficient returns to support further investment.

Policy shifts are reshaping demand

The slowdown also follows a policy change that altered how demand for energy storage is generated.

In February 2025, China’s National Development and Reform Commission and National Energy Administration scrapped a rule requiring renewable-energy projects to be paired with supporting storage capacity. Caixin reported that the mandate had helped create a predictable pipeline for battery deployment, including in cases where projects were not yet fully economical.

China has since been shifting toward market-based demand. Earlier in 2026, a national framework recognized energy storage’s capacity value. Several provinces, including Gansu, Jilin, Shaanxi, Xinjiang, Hubei, Ningxia, and Qinghai, also introduced compensation policies for storage projects.

Those measures are intended to create additional revenue opportunities, but Caixin noted that trading returns are under pressure as spreads between charging and discharging prices narrow. When those spreads shrink, it becomes harder for project owners to justify new investments.

That can affect the broader supply chain. Developers may delay projects, equipment suppliers may face pressure to cut prices, and battery-cell producers may receive fewer orders. Manufacturing capacity can continue growing even as the market’s ability to support that capacity weakens.

The freeze seems selective, not total

According to Sina Finance, local governments have largely stopped accepting new filings for additional power-battery and energy-storage-battery capacity projects since the second half of 2026. However, projects that were previously filed, approved, or already under construction can continue.

The report said consumer batteries, lithium-battery materials, supporting projects, technology upgrades, production-line retrofits, and overseas factory construction are outside the restriction. Companies with diversified operations may therefore continue certain projects even while new domestic greenfield storage plants remain on hold.

Sina sources said the approval window could reopen after authorities complete their capacity inventory and establish a capacity-monitoring and warning mechanism.

The inventory process could help authorities distinguish between projects needed by the market and those announced during the sector’s expansion. It also gives officials a way to assess proposed capacity before granting further approvals.

Margin pressure: the real issue for manufacturers

The core problem for many manufacturers is not simply how many megawatt-hours the market may require, but whether those projects can generate adequate profits. Reuters said demand for storage continues to rise because batteries are used to balance grids and provide backup power. At the same time, intense competition and falling prices are putting pressure on manufacturers.

A growing market does not automatically produce healthy returns when many suppliers compete for the same business. Reuters also noted that China’s solar manufacturers have expanded into battery energy storage as shrinking solar-panel profits and overcapacity push them toward new opportunities.

The pattern is familiar: demand grows, but supply grows faster, putting pressure on prices. In that environment, companies must show that their factories can operate efficiently and secure firm orders, rather than relying on scale alone.

Major players face a cautious domestic climate

The companies most exposed are those whose upcoming domestic projects have not yet received approval to begin construction.

The Robotics Media article named CATL, BYD, Envision, Gotion High-Tech, and Hithium as major players affected or strategically positioned in the sector. New greenfield storage plants that had not secured approval before the pause are in limbo, while registered projects already under construction can continue.

The pause is tied to an inventory of existing and planned capacity, with a focus on battery-cell manufacturing. It is not described as a blanket or necessarily permanent shutdown.

The international scene is also tightening restrictions

Chinese manufacturers are also navigating a more complicated global environment.

In the United States, an executive order issued on August 26 included energy-storage systems and grid-connected inverters among equipment subject to restrictions concerning the bulk-power system. The Energy Department can restrict transactions involving foreign-made equipment deemed to pose a security risk.

The European Union is also raising barriers to foreign energy-storage equipment in public procurement and renewable-energy auctions.

These policies could create opportunities for non-Chinese suppliers. But market access will depend on regulatory compliance, supply-chain resilience, support capabilities, and the requirements of utilities and governments, not just production volume.

So, what’s next?

The main question is whether the pause is a short-term administrative hold or the beginning of a longer effort to control capacity growth.

ESS News said no formal government decree had been published, while Reuters noted that the policy could later be adjusted. Approvals could therefore resume after authorities complete their assessments.

The capacity review, exemptions for existing and specialized projects, and efforts to address duplicate construction and price erosion all point toward more careful scrutiny of future projects.

For the global energy-storage sector, that could mean slower but more disciplined expansion, affecting sourcing, factory locations, equipment suppliers, logistics, and competition among companies seeking growth in automotive and grid-storage markets.

Key takeaways

- The reported pause appears selective, focusing mainly on new domestic battery-cell projects that have not yet begun construction.

- Existing factories, approved projects, technology upgrades, and some overseas operations may continue.

- Slower storage deployment, falling prices, and narrowing project returns are increasing pressure on manufacturers.

- The capacity review could influence future factory approvals, sourcing strategies, logistics planning, and investment decisions.

- International restrictions may encourage more regionalized electronics and battery supply chains.

- The long-term effect will depend on whether authorities resume approvals after completing their capacity assessment.

text:
NewsVoir

Gurugram (Haryana) [India], September 8: A new study strengthens the case for EVs on emissions. But in India, the winning argument may be less about saving the planet and more about making electric cars genuinely easy and appealing to own.

A new study in the journal Science gives the electric-car pitch a fresh twist: replacing a functioning gasoline car with an EV can cut lifetime emissions even before the old car reaches the end of its useful life.

Previously, the usual argument against early EV replacement has been fairly intuitive: if the gasoline car is already built, why create another manufacturing footprint just to replace it? The new research's counter: the carbon cost of making an EV can be repaid by its lower emissions during operation.

In their representative US SUV scenario, replacing the combustion vehicle in its second year cut cumulative emissions over a 16-year period by 44 percent, with the EV's manufacturing "carbon debt" paid back in three years. Across the study's modeled vehicle scenarios, 92% produced a net emissions reduction, while fleet-average assumptions delivered a 58 percent benefit.

The researchers put the underlying point rather neatly: "electrifying vehicle powertrains provides an order-of-magnitude-larger reduction in use-phase emissions" than replacing an old ICE vehicle with a newer ICE vehicle. They ultimately found "large carbon mitigation benefits across a wide range of scenarios," although the outcome still depends on vehicle efficiency, battery-production emissions and the electricity grid.

The study no doubt strengthens the case for switching from a gas-guzzling vehicle to a new EV for environmental reasons. But alas, in emerging markets like India, an EV brand that leans too heavily on that narrative will certainly fail. Indian customers are practical people and naturally seek practical mode of transportation. They are unlikely to buy a vehicle simply because it helps reduce their personal carbon footprint. A car is transport, technology, a status symbol, family space and, increasingly, an extension of personal identity.

For EVs, that makes the proposition less "save the planet" and more "this happens to make sense." OEMs should emphasize benefits such as lower running costs, quieter driving, instant torque, connected features and the ability to charge at home to turn electrification into a lifestyle upgrade rather than an environmental sacrifice.

The economics can be compelling, too. For example, VinFast's India portfolio includes the VF 6 and VF 7 SUVs, alongside the seven-seat VF MPV 7. The latter is listed at INR 2.449 million, or about INR 24.49 lakh, before incentives. Its comparison with a comparable gas-powered vehicle showed a significantly lower five-year ownership cost, even before counting free charging.

VinFast is also trying to tackle the less glamorous part of EV ownership: everything that happens after the keys are handed over.

It offers free charging at V-Green stations through March 31, 2029, alongside free scheduled maintenance for three years or 36,000 km. Customers switching from an ICE vehicle can also receive cash support ranging from INR 138,000 for the VF 6 Earth to INR 214,000 for the VF 7 Sky Infinity, with INR 196,000 available for the VF MPV 7.

Then comes the ecosystem. VinFast recently inaugurated its 60th retail outlet in India, with plans to establish 75 dealerships across more than 60 cities by the end of 2026.

Charging-wise, VinFast's strategic partner V-Green and HPCL are working to deploy EV chargers nationwide. V-Green has also partnered with RoadGrid to accelerate fast-charging deployment at fuel stations, smart cities and other high-demand locations.

The bigger point is that India's EV transition will probably be won in the details. Cleaner driving is the headline benefit, but cheaper running, useful range, easy charging, accessible service and a car that feels desirable are what can turn curiosity into ownership.

The greenest car, in other words, may increasingly be the one people actually want to drive.

VinFast is currently embarking on its next growth phase through rapid expansion of its distribution and dealership network globally and increasing its manufacturing capacities with a focus on key markets across North America, Europe, the Middle East and Asia.

title: Can SpaceX's massive Louisiana spaceport benefit coastal restoration? It's a high-stakes question.
authors: Alex Lubben, Staff, SOPHIA GERMER, CHRIS GRANGER, DAN SWENSON, Graphics Editor, LESLIE WESTBROOK
description:
SpaceX’s president and chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell pledged to carry out restoration projects in Vermilion Parish in cooperation with the state’s coastal authority.
That’s coastal restoration.
But coastal groups ask what specific investments the company will make in coastal restoration, both near the launchpads and potentially elsewhere throughout the state.
The funds from that sale are earmarked for coastal restoration in Vermilion Parish, Hare said.
Those boats are crucial to many coastal restoration efforts and they can’t be in two places at once.
text:
A plan to build what may be the world’s largest spaceport would be supremely ambitious for any location.

But in the marshes of south Louisiana, where a football field of land disappears every 100 minutes, Elon Musk’s grand vision for SpaceX will be confronted with unique challenges.

On top of the technical considerations of building what Musk calls Starbase Louisiana near Pecan Island, coastal restoration groups will be watching closely to see how the project fits into the state’s long struggle against land loss.

SpaceX’s president and chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell pledged to carry out restoration projects in Vermilion Parish in cooperation with the state’s coastal authority.

“The work includes thousands of acres of marsh creation to reconnect fragmented wetlands and help restore the natural storm buffer that this coast has lost,” she said.

But the scale of the project and the complex circumstances surrounding it have raised a host of questions whose answers are not yet clear.

They include how a settlement in a lawsuit over coastal damage, through which SpaceX has acquired access to the land, will ultimately benefit restoration efforts. A separate issue involves how a federal push to speed the regulatory approval process for aerospace developments may affect the project.

Work to restore the state’s coastline has long been viewed as vital in south Louisiana. There are hopes that SpaceX’s plans will serve as a win-win, stoking economic development while providing needed restoration dollars, but there are few details so far of how the company will contribute.

“As a new arrival to our state, SpaceX will share the responsibility to protect our coast,” said Kim Reyher, executive director of the Coalition to Restore Coastal Louisiana, the state’s oldest coastal advocacy organization.

Referring to the state's 50-year blueprint for salvaging as much land as possible, Reyher said: “An investment of this magnitude must bring significant new resources to protect and restore the wetlands of the region and accelerate implementation of Coastal Master Plan projects.”

Michael Hare, executive director of the state's Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority, said that SpaceX has proactively worked with his agency since March to formulate plans to maintain the coast and mitigate impacts the new spaceport may have.

“I believe their overall investment is going to accelerate coastal restoration in this area at a pace that we would have never been able to accomplish had they not come,” Hare said, adding that he appreciated that the project would provoke “legitimate public concern.”

“I have confidence in our regulatory agencies to enforce our rules, our regulations, to the highest standards,” he said.

The massive $100 billion spaceport could be among the largest launch sites in the history of spaceflight. It is slated for construction in a rural area that’s historically been a duck hunting hotspot, a fragile part of the coastline that has lost wetlands in recent decades and is expected to lose more as sea levels rise.

An investment that size gives SpaceX a strong reason to keep its land from eroding. To Vermilion Parish President Chad Vallo, that alone could provide significant storm surge protection for the region.

“They’re not going to put their site in a place where there’s one storm and they’re going to lose it. That’s coastal restoration. That’s protecting Pecan Island, all the way up to Gueydan,” he said. “I think just their site is going to offer a huge amount of protection.”

'Lack of transparency'

Louisiana has lost an area the size of Delaware since the 1930s, a crisis driven by compounding factors. Since the early 20th century, the Mississippi River has been straitjacketed by levees and no longer overflows its banks as it used to, starving wetlands of the sediment needed to replenish them. Sea level rise has also contributed, as have oil and gas companies, by cutting canals through the marsh and accelerating subsidence through fossil fuel extraction.

The state’s plan to protect the coast involves dozens of projects that include marsh creation, barrier island restoration, and, until recently, large-scale sediment diversions that would have allowed the river to flow back into wetlands. Under Landry, diversion plans have been scuttled in favor of other projects, like marsh creation and rock jetties.

But coastal groups ask what specific investments the company will make in coastal restoration, both near the launchpads and potentially elsewhere throughout the state. Those details may have remained out of sight because state officials close to the project have signed nondisclosure agreements to maintain the confidentiality of negotiations with the company.

“A lot of the frustration, from my point of view, lies in the lack of transparency in all of this,” said Alisha Renfro, a coastal scientist with the National Wildlife Federation. “How do you minimize impacts? We’re all flying around blind.”

As part of the development of the spaceport, SpaceX acknowledges that some wetlands will be damaged. The company has acquired around 125,000 acres of land along the coast, about 40,000 of which it plans to develop as part of its new launch site, according to the company. Building it will likely involve expanding roads, or filling in new land in areas that are now marsh.

Mark Davis, an environmental law professor at Tulane University, noted the Federal Aviation Administration’s proposal to waive 13 laws that form the backbone of the U.S. permitting and environmental regulatory framework from applying to aerospace developments, including the Clean Water Act.

If that law is waived, he said SpaceX might not have to protect other marsh areas when it fills in wetlands around its new launch site through a process called mitigation, which is largely governed by the Clean Water Act.

“If we’re going to do this, I hope it goes well,” Davis said. But he questioned the result "if you're not doing mitigation under the Clean Water Act, where there are protocols for how you calculate the amount of mitigation, where the mitigation is supposed to be."

Hare pushed back, saying that regardless of the FAA rule, the spaceport will be subject to the Clean Water Act.

“They’re still going to have to go through their normal permitting process. It will require mitigation,” he said. “I don’t think there’s any question of that whatsoever."

'Trump speed'

Landry, SpaceX and federal officials have all stressed that the company will voluntarily contribute to the state’s coastal restoration initiatives, regardless of whether it’s required to do so.

Adam Telle, until recently the assistant secretary of the Army for Civil Works and just promoted to acting secretary of the Army, said he intended for the development of the spaceport to move at “Trump speed” without overlooking environmental considerations.

“We follow the law. We do what the law says,” he said during a recent visit to Grand Isle. “The law doesn’t say you have to think about it for a long time. It says you can look at it, look at the facts, and make a decision.”

SpaceX also secured its launch site in lower Vermilion Parish through a settlement in a coastal lawsuit against ExxonMobil, which alleged that the company damaged the state’s coastline. Exxon turned 125,000 acres of land over to the state as part of that settlement, and SpaceX paid the state $100 million for it. The funds from that sale are earmarked for coastal restoration in Vermilion Parish, Hare said.

But it is not clear whether the state received additional funds from Exxon as part of the settlement because its details are sealed by court order. As a comparison, the state's Coastal Master Plan calls for $1 billion per year in projects over 50 years to keep up with accelerating land loss. The state also faces a sharp drop in restoration funding when BP oil spill money runs out in 2032.

How will the state work with SpaceX?

It’s also not yet clear how SpaceX will work alongside CPRA on its restoration efforts. The details have yet to be determined, Hare said.

“Do they want us to build and they pay us back for it? Possibly,” Hare said. “Do they want to make sure they get all of our best design standards and understanding? Or they design it and then maybe they send it to us for review and they want to make sure that we're always viewing it from a consistency standpoint? I think that's possible as well.”

To some coastal advocates, that way of working raises questions about whether the state is sidelining its own plans, painstakingly developed in a yearslong process.

“Is CPRA expecting to do specific projects for coastal restoration or protection that benefit the SpaceX site in Louisiana?” asked Rebecca Triche, the executive director of the Louisiana Wildlife Federation. “Is it really coastal restoration if we end up with net loss of wetlands and reduced wetlands functions and values for wildlife and fish?”

Hare said that the state has ample coastal resources to build a spaceport and restore the coast simultaneously. He stressed that his agency would not perform work on behalf of SpaceX and that the spaceport’s construction will not interfere with any of CPRA’s planned coastal projects.

Still, the U.S. only has about two dozen active hopper dredges, the types of boats capable of carrying out marsh-building projects, which may be needed to build out the spaceport, according to Megan Biven, founder of True Transition, an energy industry research group. Those boats are crucial to many coastal restoration efforts and they can’t be in two places at once.

“The state’s Master Plan is Louisiana’s moonshot to save itself,” Biven said.

title: Germany's far right alternative energy reality - POLITICO
description:
