title: We Need Renewable Energy Fast, and Ways to get the Public On Board
description:
To address this, the obvious solution is to build more renewable energy projects and the transmission infrastructure to connect them at scale.
However, regional communities should not be forced to choose between supporting the national energy transition and protecting their land and livelihoods.
Instead of querying “if” communities support renewable energy, we should be asking “under what conditions” will they back such projects.
Lessons from abroad Overseas, other countries are already trialling ways of giving host communities a more tangible stake in the renewable energy shift.
Mingming Cheng, Professor, School of Management and Marketing, Curtin University and Peta Ashworth, Professor and Director, Curtin Institute for Energy Transition, Curtin University
text:
By Mingming Cheng, Curtin University and Peta Ashworth, Curtin University

(The Conversation) – Australia’s energy transition has never been more urgent.

Aging coal-fired power stations are retiring and energy bills are rising sharply. To address this, the obvious solution is to build more renewable energy projects and the transmission infrastructure to connect them at scale.

But a major hurdle remains: community opposition. In regional areas, where most of the renewable infrastructure must go, locals are protesting against new transmission lines and are locking farm gates to keep developers off their property.

However, regional communities should not be forced to choose between supporting the national energy transition and protecting their land and livelihoods.

Our new research suggests we’re asking the wrong question. Instead of querying “if” communities support renewable energy, we should be asking “under what conditions” will they back such projects.

Not simply for or against

Our new study took a closer look at how three regional Western Australian communities – Busselton, Kojonup and Albany – view renewable energy infrastructure.

To do this, we analysed online discussions about solar and wind projects slated for their communities, each at different stages of development. The online discussions took place from January 2024 to May 2025 across a range of platforms, including Facebook and X (formerly Twitter), as well as relevant local and regional media websites, newspapers, community forums and online noticeboards.

Our results challenge the assumption that communities can simply be divided into those who are “for” clean energy and those who are adamantly “against” it.

In Busselton on WA’s south-west tip, renewable projects are still in the planning stage. There, local residents were most concerned about land use, property values and the visual appeal of landscapes. Many residents raised consultation as a key issue, with some expressing the view consultation came too late or did not give residents any opportunity to influence the outcome.

In the inland town of Kojonup, south-east of Perth, the Kojonup wind farm is currently being rolled out. This community’s concerns were decidedly practical: who actually gets the jobs? Who receives the financial benefits? Who bears any disruptions, such as visual disruption and lower property values? Financial fairness was a major concern for locals, with some landowners receiving benefits such as local investment opportunities while their neighbours got nothing except interrupted views.

The port city of Albany has been home to working wind farms for more than two decades. Here, the picture is very different. Albany’s wind farm supplies the equivalent of 80% of the city’s annual electricity needs and attracts an estimated 200,000 visitors a year. Community sentiment was largely positive, associating the wind farm with various environmental benefits including reduced reliance on coal and gas, as well as tourism and regional identity.

It’s worth noting not every host community will embrace renewable energy in such a linear pattern. However, our findings suggest community support is not necessarily fixed and can change over time as a project progresses.

Lessons from abroad

Overseas, other countries are already trialling ways of giving host communities a more tangible stake in the renewable energy shift.

Since 2014, the Scottish government recommends wind developers pay a minimum of £5,000 (roughly A$9500) annually for each megawatt of power a renewable project generates.

These payments are channelled into community funds, where a local committee decides how the funds are spent. If a project stretches across multiple regions, the funds are split based on how many megawatts of power each community hosts. However, these payments are not mandatory so not all renewable companies are contributing to community funds.

In Denmark, a global leader in wind energy development, several communities have established energy cooperatives. While each has a slightly different model, these cooperatives allow residents to own a share of renewable energy projects and, as a result, actively engage in the green transition.

Where to from here

These international examples underscore the need to engage with host communities in innovative and thoughtful ways.

Our research suggests these three strategies could help:

Photo of Cairns by David Clode on Unsplash

recognising that if people resist local solar and wind projects, they are not simply “anti-renewables”

engaging communities early, listening to their concerns about proposed renewable projects, involving them in decision-making processes and providing clear, transparent information about how any risks will be managed and benefits will be shared

monitoring online discussions, particularly to identify emerging concerns before they become entrenched as opposition and potentially fracture trust between communities, government and renewables companies.

Australia, like many countries, is racing to shore up its renewable sector and shift away from fossil fuels. We must build more wind turbines and solar farms. But to ensure our energy transition works, building trust with local communities is just as crucial.

Mingming Cheng, Professor, School of Management and Marketing, Curtin University and Peta Ashworth, Professor and Director, Curtin Institute for Energy Transition, Curtin University

text:
By Leila Miller

BUENOS AIRES, Sept 7 (Reuters) – Argentina’s rugged Patagonia is drawing increasing interest from investors searching for sites for mega data centers who are enticed by the region’s cool temperatures, renewable energy, shale gas and empty stretches of land.

As tech giants known as hyperscalers race worldwide to build server farms and run into roadblocks amid anti-data-center campaigns, projects in initial stages in Argentina are developing without much public attention. Since Argentines have yet to be impacted by large data centers, the country lacks a backlash against the server farms as in the U.S., where critics say they strain local power grids, harm ​the environment and increase utility bills. Supporters say the facilities are essential for the AI boom, generate significant local tax revenue, and can be made more sustainable.

The Patagonia region is at South America’s southern tip, ‌known for its jagged mountain peaks, desert landscapes and massive glaciers. In Argentina’s province of Neuquen, located in Patagonia, major electricity generator Pampa Energia is pushing for a data center that would be located by the company’s Loma de la Lata thermal power plant. It would consume up to 500 megawatts of energy from nearby Vaca Muerta, one of the world’s largest shale gas formations, said Ruben Turienzo, the company’s commercial director for electricity.

Mapuche Indigenous families live in the rural area, and have historically clashed with energy companies. Pampa began studying the project, which was previously unreported, after receiving inquiries at the beginning of this year about potential data center projects.

“We started to detect there was interest that was a bit firmer,” said Turienzo.

MILEI’S REFORMS ATTRACT INVESTORS

The attention on Argentina comes amid a steadier macroeconomy in a country historically plagued by high inflation. Under President ‌Javier Milei, ​who took office in December 2023, Argentina has attracted major oil and mining investments through the RIGI incentive regime, which provides tax breaks and regulatory stability, while ⁠strengthening ties with Washington.

“Two years ago, nobody would talk about Argentina,” ⁠said Steve Sasse, vice president for Latin America at datacenterHawk, a Texas-based market intelligence group.

OpenAI announced last October that it would partner with local company Sur Energy on a data center powered by clean energy costing up to $25 billion, with a capacity of up to 500 MW. In July, Argentina’s communications agency said it intends to create a second fiber-optic cable landing station to make Patagonia friendlier to data centers.

Argentina now has only small data centers, concentrated in Buenos Aires. It lags behind its neighbors. Amazon.com is moving ahead on a mega data center in Chile, while Alphabet’s Google constructs one in Uruguay. In May, Paraguay shared plans for a data center with ​backing from Taiwan.

“Everyone is looking for power, that’s why international developers are looking at Argentina,” said Hadassa Lutz, co-founder of Cloud2Ground, a U.S. advisory firm for data centers. “But saying you have power is not enough.”

Some investors may wait for Argentina’s 2027 presidential election and are watching Milei’s proposed Super RIGI, another legislative framework with larger tax cuts.

“If that uncertainty clarifies and we now have a bankable option in Argentina, investors will take the risk,” said Lutz.

PATAGONIA LURE

Pampa Energia is quoting energy ⁠prices to interested parties and aims to reach initial agreements by the end of 2026, said Turienzo. Investors first want a smaller pilot, ⁠20 MW to 40 MW, before expanding. The electric infrastructure for 500 MW would cost almost $900 million, he said.

Neuquen offers a cold climate that lowers cooling costs and access to ​both hydroelectric power and Vaca Muerta gas, said Ruben Etcheverry, secretary of the province’s development council.

“What we envision is a data center cluster or ecosystem, where once the first facility is established it’ll dispel preconceptions and risks,” he said.

Etcheverry has fielded inquiries ​from parties including FlexDomes, a U.S.-based green data center company looking for investors for a Neuquen data center. The first stage for 120 MW of IT load would cost $1.4 billion ‌and use Vaca Muerta energy, said Gabriel Obrador, who represents the company in Argentina.

Meanwhile, in the southern province of Chubut, Poland’s Green Capital said in July it is planning a data center that in the first stage would reach 300 MW, costing $3 billion, but could ultimately reach 3,000 MW, according to Marta Złotkowska, its head of international development and data centers. It is currently leasing about 501 square miles (1,298 square km) of land south of the city of Trelew to build wind and solar farms — the project aims to avoid using the national grid — but needs investors and plans to apply for an investment regime in 2027.

In Buenos Aires province, companies are also scouring sites. Pampa Energia has agreed to provide 30 MW for the first stage ⁠of a data center in a free trade zone in the city of Bahia Blanca, known for its wind power. Pablo Amarelle, general manager of the zone’s concessionaire, said the company has begun constructing an IT park and expects final investment agreements by late 2026.

Hyperscalers leasing space are weighing expansion, exploring “possibilities that were previously unfeasible,” said Ariel Graizer, president of the Argentina Internet Chamber.

INFRASTRUCTURE CHALLENGES

While Patagonia has energy resources and a favorable climate, infrastructure and connectivity remain hurdles.

“It’s not a ⁠product looking for a buyer — someone has to build it,” said Lutz, the consultant.

Experts caution against ‌conflating announcements with firm projects.

“There is interest, and there are plenty of players, but the project has to get started,” said Gustavo Castagnino, director of corporate affairs at ⁠Genneia, Argentina’s leading renewable energy company.

Luis Schilling, Latin America co-chair for iMasons, a U.S. nonprofit that connects digital infrastructure professionals, has postponed three times a trip for companies ​to tour sites in ‌Patagonia. It is now set for February.

“They would feel more comfortable if Milei was re-elected,” he said.

In fact, Milei has worked to court Big Tech.

In May 2024, ​he traveled to Silicon ⁠Valley to meet with Apple’s then-CEO, Tim Cook, as well as with chief executives Sam Altman of OpenAI, Sundar Pichai of Google and Mark Zuckerberg of Meta Platforms to encourage investment, including in Patagonia. Billionaire investor Peter Thiel bought a 1% stake in Vista Energy, a leading oil producer operating in Vaca Muerta, according to an August regulatory filing.

Argentina “previously wasn’t really on the map,” said Martin Varsavsky, an Argentine founder of five so-called unicorns, or startups valued at more than $1 billion. “It was like planting the Argentine flag, saying, ‘Here lies a country with abundant energy and excellent conditions for investment.”

Altman announced the OpenAI project 17 months later. Sur Energy co-founder Emiliano Kargieman and OpenAI did not respond to interview requests from Reuters. In August, Kargieman told Bloomberg Linea that he was working with Neuquen province to identify a site and “the ball is in OpenAI’s court right now to sign the definitive contract and launch the project.”

He did not know if Argentina’s upcoming election was a factor: “It’s a question for OpenAI.”

(Reporting by Leila Miller ​in Buenos Aires; Editing by Lucinda Elliott and Matthew Lewis)

title: Delaware at-home solar initiative aims to reduce energy bills - WHYY
description:
As energy bills continue to soar, Delaware is taking new steps to help more residents save money by connecting to solar power.
The goal is to lower energy bills, decrease the state’s greenhouse gas emissions and reduce strain on the electric grid.
The move repealed the Residential Clean Energy Credit, which covers up to 30% of the cost of installing qualified clean energy properties, such as solar energy projects.
Reducing energy bills Families are struggling to keep up with the cost of keeping the lights on.
The interest rate remains the same at 3.9% Delaware SHINES aims to help reduce the financial barriers to accessing solar.
text:
This story is part of the WHYY News Climate Desk, bringing you news and solutions for our changing region.

From the Poconos to the Jersey Shore to the mouth of the Delaware Bay, what do you want to know about climate change? What would you like us to cover? Get in touch.

As energy bills continue to soar, Delaware is taking new steps to help more residents save money by connecting to solar power.

Gov. Matt Meyer announced last week what he calls the “most comprehensive” solar and battery storage program in the U.S.

The initiative, dubbed Delaware SHINES, will offer grants, loans and rebates to help residents, small businesses and nonprofits utilize solar energy generation and battery storage. The goal is to lower energy bills, decrease the state’s greenhouse gas emissions and reduce strain on the electric grid.

The initiative, which stands for “Solar + Storage Home Incentive Network for Economic Stability,” comes about a year after the Trump administration dismantled parts of the Inflation Reduction Act, which provides incentives for green energy. The move repealed the Residential Clean Energy Credit, which covers up to 30% of the cost of installing qualified clean energy properties, such as solar energy projects.

“We understand that what is being done in Washington is neither based on sound energy science, nor economic policy,” Meyer said during an interview with WHYY News. “If you want to reduce costs for Delawareans and Americans, if you want to sustain the environment for generations to come, we should be incentivizing solar and wind and other renewable energy forms.”

The price per unit of energy, as well as the price to deliver energy to households, has increased significantly – driving energy companies like Delmarva Power to raise peoples’ bills.

Prices for grid operator PJM Interconnection’s capacity auction, a complex pricing system that guarantees future electricity supply, have increased significantly because of a supply-demand imbalance, increased demand from AI data centers and slow construction for new energy generation.

The energy needed to power data centers, large facilities that house servers that fuel artificial intelligence and cloud computing, has led some states to pass laws preventing those costs from being handed down to residents.

Experts say at-home solar and battery storage can reduce the load, decreasing open-market power purchases.

“Anything that you can do to generate your own electricity, as well as reduce your consumption, which is the cheapest and cleanest thing to do, can be beneficial,” said Drew Slater, executive director of Energize Delaware, which is helping to coordinate Delaware SHINES. “Because I don’t think their prices are going to come down anytime soon at the PJM market, which is a significant part of your everyday bill.”

Meyer said one of his goals is to ensure Delaware produces more of its own power. About 60% of the state’s total electricity is brought in from out-of-state power suppliers through the PJM grid.

Reducing energy bills

Families are struggling to keep up with the cost of keeping the lights on. In 2024, there were more than 30,000 electric service disconnections in Delaware because of unpaid bills, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Households that use solar can benefit from significant energy savings, but the amount varies based on a household’s size and power usage. The process works through net-metering, which credits homeowners and businesses for the excess electricity their solar panels send back to the grid.

Russell Pfaller, operations manager at Green Street Solar, said people who finance solar systems typically see a full return on their investment before their loan is over.

“It does vary per individual, but if you’re paying cash and not paying any interest at all, if you are a Delmarva Power customer with a relatively good exposure to the sun, it’s not unreasonable to see a six-year, five-year, return on investment,” he said.

At-home solar generates electricity from sunlight, while battery storage saves that surplus electricity for later use. Batteries allow residents to store energy and use it when they lose connection to the grid. In states that have higher energy rates during certain times of the day, residents can use their batteries to save money.

In the future, the program may also make way for virtual power plants on peoples’ roofs. Virtual power plants utilize solar panels, batteries, electric vehicle chargers and smart thermostats that are linked together by software to operate like a single, large power plant.

Delaware SHINES will utilize existing energy programs in the state to expand access to at-home solar and battery storage.

The state’s Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control will use increased Green Energy Fund grants to help make installing solar projects more affordable for residents.

The program, which began in 1999, offers financial rebates and incentives for the installation of renewable energy systems. The program this year raised residential solar rebates from $6,000 to $10,000.

Delaware SHINES will also be coordinated by the state’s Energize Delaware program. Funded by the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, it offers energy audits, financial incentives and low interest financing to help residents and businesses connect to solar.

Slater said the nonprofit saw a spike in demand for its services in the weeks before the federal tax credits expired. Since then, it has increased its loan maximum from $30,000 to $50,000. The loans now cover 100% of a project’s cost, and its terms have increased to up to 15 years. The interest rate remains the same at 3.9%

Delaware SHINES aims to help reduce the financial barriers to accessing solar.

“In the past, there’s always been an argument, ‘I have to pay more for the solar than I’d be paying for the electricity from the grid,’ or ‘I’m basically paying the same thing,’” Pfaller said. “These [Delaware SHINES] incentives bring you to a place where it actually does make sense on paper.”

In addition to lowering energy bills, Meyer said the plan will create jobs in the energy sector and help the state meet its goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 50% by 2030.

“We’re increasing affordability while reducing the impact on climate, reducing the reliance on fossil fuels and on gas and the oil powered energy,” he said. “Every rooftop system is power generated, not through importation from another state or country, its emissions not produced, and its money very directly kept in Delaware family’s pockets when climate policy and kitchen table economics point in the same direction.”

title: Copper supply chain decarbonization for the energy transition must maximize copper recovery
description:
In efforts to reduce global carbon emissions, net-zero carbon has become a primary environmental focus of most major industries, governments, and many multilateral organizations4,5.
As a result of this context, the copper industry is faced with two climate energy transition goals: (1) to produce enough new marginal copper supply to support the global energy transition’s technological solutions, while (2) eliminating the copper industry’s carbon emissions.
Carbon copper recovery trade-off The life cycle of copper production has an average carbon footprint of 4.2 tonnes per tonne of metal produced9.
Prioritizing systems-level copper recovery To illustrate why it is so important to prioritize systems-level copper recovery, we consider the DEP benefits of a flowchart design that can achieve a hypothetical 1% and a 5% increase in systems recovery.
The cost of compromising copper recovery The above analysis clearly illustrates the importance of optimizing recovery across copper production systems.
text:
To limit the damage from global warming, a fundamental and rapid transition in energy generation, storage, and consumption is urgently required. Solutions such as Photovoltaic Energy (PV), Wind Power (WP), Electric Vehicles (EV), and Battery Electric Storage Systems (BESS) are essential for providing and storing the renewable energy that can replace fossil fuels1. Due to being a crucial supplier of core building materials such as copper, nickel, lithium, cobalt, and rare earth elements2, the metals and mining industry is uniquely positioned as an enabler of the global energy transition2. Some of these metals, such as copper, are recognized as being geologically and economically scarce, thus representing a supply risk to global climate goals2,3.

In efforts to reduce global carbon emissions, net-zero carbon has become a primary environmental focus of most major industries, governments, and many multilateral organizations4,5. As of June 2024, 107 countries have pledged to achieve net-zero emissions6, and in 2023, 1.78 trillion dollars was spent on climate change mitigation7. The three types of emissions being targeted for all industries are direct emissions (Scope 1), electricity-based grid emissions (Scope 2), and downstream emissions, which result from the further use of products and services (Scope 3). The primary technological solutions for the reduction of Scope 2 emissions are PV, WP, and BESS, all of which are copper-intensive technologies8. Furthermore, these technologies require a shift in how electricity is generated and stored, resulting in more decentralized, grid-based energy networks, which are also inherently copper-intensive.

Material flow analyses confirm the crucial role of copper in reducing Scope 2 and Scope 3 emissions9. There are also no interchangeable and fungible substitutes for most PV, WP, BESS, and EV copper use due to its excellent conductivity and lifecycle environmental performance10. Copper is geologically constrained; growing demand for copper is likely to lead to the development of new mines and increased supplies11. However, a lack of new large ore body discoveries and a limited new mining project pipeline, coupled with an 18-year average time to build a new mine (from discovery to production), will lead to limited medium-term supply growth11,12. Brownfield expansions of existing mines and an increase in identified reserves through new exploration with a growth in copper price is expected to drive a considerable share of the near-term supply growth13. However, brownfield expansions come with limits on extraction due to an increased footprint on regions already impacted by mining, and can lead to intensifying social conflict, political risk, and local environmental opposition14.

At the same time, the mining industry is not immune to global pressure towards large-scale decarbonization efforts. The mining sector is recognized as being a significant CO2-equivalent (CO2e) emitter, accounting for 4–7% of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions15. Following the Paris Accord and other international and industry-wide policy movements towards decarbonization goals, the copper industry15, including companies with major copper assets such as BHP16 and Rio Tinto17, have prioritized the adoption of net-zero goals and technologies that support long-term decarbonization of projects18.

As a result of this context, the copper industry is faced with two climate energy transition goals: (1) to produce enough new marginal copper supply to support the global energy transition’s technological solutions, while (2) eliminating the copper industry’s carbon emissions. In this paper, we suggest that these goals result in a sustainability dilemma, i.e., the emphasis on decarbonizing copper mines poses an unintended consequence for the ability to secure global copper supply chains. This is because at every stage of the production process, there is a potential trade-off between the recovery of metal and the embedded carbon footprint.

Previous models in the literature on carbon footprint reduction in copper production from primary sulfides for the energy transition have metallurgical recovery as a fixed variable2,19. In this paper, a new conceptual metric, Decarbonization Enabling Potential (DEP), is proposed that values marginal recovery as a variable. The production and carbon metric compares the carbon footprint savings from recovery-based reductions in mining industry carbon emissions with the downstream value-in-use emission reductions from using copper. The value-in-use emission reductions are modeled across the four major sustainable energy enabling technologies and technology packages: PV, WP, BESS, and EV’s. Based on this illustrative analysis, there is a compelling argument that any reduction in system recovery resulting from emissions-reduction initiatives in the copper mining and smelting industry may be counterproductive to reducing global carbon emissions, because copper is an important enabling input for sustainable energy technologies. Put another way, this systems-level metric shows that the copper industry could prioritize recovery from the ore body to the smelter to maximise the value of copper-in-use in support of the global energy transition. Decarbonization efforts for that sector should prioritize solutions that increase, or at least do not decrease, mineral recovery, such as transitioning to sustainable energy sources or reducing emissions during transportation.

Decarbonization enabling potential

Table 1 illustrates the modeled decarbonization enabling potential (DEP) per tonne of copper, broken down by energy transition solutions. The DEP was calculated by taking the net carbon savings of the technology over its life cycle and then dividing it by the copper intensity per MW installed or per EV.

There are some aspects of the DEP conceptualization that are important to highlight. First, it is recognized that circularity will be key to sustaining the energy transition. This paper views recovery of recycled copper as important to the energy transition, but the authors feel that primary production will be required to initiate the decarbonization process. PV, WP, EV, and BESS need to be manufactured, deployed, and then recycled before there is anything to recycle, a process that may take decades depending on the technology. However, there is a case that was not modeled where secondary copper supply for new PV, WP, or BESS could be sourced from copper already in service and nearing the end of its life. Similarly, for infrastructure that could be recycled with limited replacement at the same copper intensity. An example of where circularity could deliver marginal copper is a copper transmission line being replaced with an aluminum one. The authors base case circular economy assumption is that recycled copper was contained in infrastructure or products that will be replaced with other infrastructure with similar copper intensity. It is envisaged that the replacement infrastructure will need that recycled copper and will therefore not be available for re-deployment in new PV, WP, or BESS systems. Therefore, the DEP of new and recycled copper entering the supply system will increase as copper intensity in PV, WP, or BESS decreases. Over time, we also expect circularity to mature, other copper users to potentially reduce their copper dependence (e.g.,20), and copper containing infrastructure approach end of life. Those cases may enable additional copper to be available for supporting the energy transition21, and the DEP of copper may then lose its significance if it is no longer a limiting factor. However, for the purposes of the modeling presented in this paper, DEP is scoped to the first cycle of use, defined from deployment to end of expected life with 0% recycling assumed. This is the most conservative DEP ratio, and the most important DEP case to model for short term climate goals.

Second, the DEP ratio is defined such that 100% of the Decarbonization Enabling Potential is attributed to copper. It does this because copper has limited interchangeable, fungible substitutes for most energy transition solutions, and as such, it is argued that copper is a core limiting factor on society’s ability to enact the energy transition. The purpose of the DEP ratio is to understand copper’s enabling potential to inform systems-level decision making and to illustrate the importance of maximizing copper recovery. It is important to highlight that this analysis therefore does not suggest that all carbon savings should be attributed to copper for purposes such as CO2 reporting and accounting, or CO2 offsets.

Finally, it is important to recognize that the DEP of copper is sensitive to the intensity of copper use within energy transition technologies. Therefore, DEP can vary depending on, for example, how PV is configured, decisions about future grid infrastructure design, which may affect energy yields and associated carbon savings. It is a comparison between two energy solutions, for example, PV and natural gas, or WP and coal generated power. As PV gets more efficient in converting solar radiation into electricity the DEP will go up, or if a new PV solution is implemented with less copper per watt installed that also will increase the DEP.

There are two unlikely boundary scenarios that would limit or eliminate the relevance of the DEP for copper. First, if copper could be entirely substituted within new energy transition technologies, then its DEP would simplify to zero. This is, for example, what occurred in the case of cobalt. It was considered a difficult-to-replace input to EV battery cathodes, but alternative chemistries have since reduced or eliminated cobalt requirements22. Second, if copper were no longer geologically constrained (e.g., if abundant new geological deposits or new net supply sources were uncovered), then copper may no longer be a limiting factor in the deployment of energy transition solutions and as such, the DEP would be irrelevant.

The influence of innovation on copper’s DEP represents a fruitful area for future research but is outside of the scope of this initial conceptual paper.

$${DEP}({RE})=\frac{({{CO}}_{2}e\,{footprint}\,{natural}\,{gas}-{{CO}}_{2}e\,{footprint}\,{RE})}{\left[\frac{{Cu}\,{intensity}\,{per}\,{MW}\,{installed}\,{RE}-{Cu}\,{intensity}\,{per}\,{MW}\,{installed}\,{natural}\,{gas}}{{Capacity}\,{factor}\,{or}\,{production}\,{ratio}\,x\,{lifespan}\,{in}\,{yrs}\,}\right]}$$

$${DEP}({EV})=\frac{({{CO}}_{2}e\,{footprint}\,{ICE}-{{CO}}_{2}e\,{footprint}\,{EV})}{({Cu}\,{intensity}\,{EV}-{Cu}\,{intensity}\,{ICE})}$$

The technologies are selected based on their maturity and market success. Combined, the sustainable energy technologies represent partial solutions for reducing global GHG emissions from the use of coal, natural gas, and fuel oils for energy production. This is significant because energy production for electricity, heat and transport systems is estimated to collectively account for 73.2% of all global GHG23. The results of the DEP model (Table 1) show the impact of increased copper deployment on CO2e savings through use in sustainable energy technologies. A single tonne of copper results in a DEP of over 8900 tonnes CO2e for PV (without battery storage) and over 30,000 tonnes CO2e for onshore wind. In the case of PV, when combined with battery storage technologies, the DEP decreases, which is dependent on the degree of integration with battery storage, but nonetheless remains noteworthy. For example, the DEP from supplying one tonne of copper for PV + 3x BESS technologies equates to 2676 tonnes CO2e, which is roughly equivalent to the annualized carbon emissions of 582 gasoline-powered passenger vehicles a typical passenger vehicle emits ~4.6 metric tons of CO2e /year24.

Carbon copper recovery trade-off

The life cycle of copper production has an average carbon footprint of 4.2 tonnes per tonne of metal produced9. This footprint includes mining, milling, transportation, smelting, and waste disposal, as well as ventilation and heating, especially in cold climates. By comparing this number with Table 1, it is already clear that the DEP of copper-in-use for sustainable energy technologies far exceeds the carbon emissions generated during copper production. In this section, we consider how the copper industry can continue to pursue large-scale decarbonization efforts without compromising the delivery of the copper needed for sustainable energy technologies.

The majority of the world’s copper is produced from sulfide ore, representing around 80% of global production25. For the purpose of this discussion, refining copper metal from a copper sulfide ore-body will be broken into three stages as can be seen in Fig. 1.

(1)

The first stage begins with mining the rock containing the ore from the ground. Usually the rock is blasted then this broken rock is removed and hauled to a location (typically on the same site) for further processing. This stage typically consumes 16–21% of the total energy required to produce copper26,27. Cut-off grades determine what rock is considered ore (i.e. containing the valuable mineral) and what rock is considered waste rock. The cut-off grade is the minimum grade of metal in the rock that can be mined and processed economically. It is usually determined by an iterative process which compares several factors, including costs, metallurgical recoveries, operational capacities, and revenues28,29. Typically, the approach for setting the cut-off grade seeks to maximize economic value for the operation and mine owner28 and does not consider the downstream value-in-use or DEP potential of the metal produced. In other words, the overall ‘systems recovery’ from orebody to smelter is not usually a primary consideration in decisions about cut-off grade.

(2)

The second stage entails separating the copper-sulfide minerals from the ore to produce a final copper-sulfide-rich mineral concentrate. This stage, commonly referred to as beneficiation, involves crushing and grinding ores to fine grains to break apart the rock to followed by the separation of the desired minerals. The flotation process is then the most common approach used to separate the copper-sulfide minerals from the others on the basis of surface chemistry. The recovered copper continues through the processing circuit to produce copper concentrate, while the undesired minerals and any unrecovered copper containing minerals are deposited in a tailings storage facility. Together, these processes utilize 43–45% of the overall energy needed to produce copper metal, the bulk of this energy being used to break the rock to the required size (crushing and grinding)26,27. For a given ore body, an operation will target a specific concentrate grade and metallurgical recovery. Ultimately, this relationship determines the overall energy required during Stage 2.

(3)

The final stage involves smelting the copper-sulfide concentrate to produce copper metal. Smelting typically consumes 36–39% of the overall energy required to produce copper, with the bulk used to heat the concentrate to a molten state26,27. To reduce the smelting carbon footprint, it is necessary to produce a higher-grade, lower-impurity concentrate with a high sulfur content. Generally, the higher the concentrate grade, the lower the smelter’s carbon footprint30. However, to achieve a higher concentrate grade, it is necessary to send copper minerals with complex associations or mineralogy to tailings, in stage 2, at the expense of system-level recovery31.

Within this value chain, multiple decisions have been made that impact the recovery of copper and the net emissions across the production system. This creates a challenge because there is a segregation of control and ownership over the three stages described above such that decisions are often made to optimize each stage independently, usually on an economic basis, which may not necessarily be optimal when considering the entire copper production system. For example, an exclusive focus on reducing the energy footprint of the beneficiation stage may result in some copper being diverted to waste streams too early which will in turn reduce systems-level recovery. If there were a better shared understanding of the importance of copper recovery to the reduction of global CO2e emissions, it is argued that a common goal could be defined that incentivizes behavior in each stage to maximize system-level copper recovery from orebody to smelter while also reducing the carbon emissions of the copper flowsheet (Fig. 1) itself. Such solutions could include, for example, adjusting ore/waste grade cut off, shifting the grind size, optimizing mill energy consumption, and smelters being open to accepting a lower concentrate grade. Further examples of solutions that can improve overall systems recovery include employing bulk ore sorting technology to reduce the chances of valuable metal being misclassified and ending up in waste piles32, additions to existing flotation cells such as froth crowding33 or selective magnetic agglomeration34. These are in addition to more traditional optimization methods such as improved process control, improved reagents and ensuring optimum grind-size.

Quantifying the balance between the metal recovery in various stages of the copper production value-chain and overall system recovery (hereafter referred to as “systems recovery”) is a key metric in the DEP model.

Prioritizing systems-level copper recovery

To illustrate why it is so important to prioritize systems-level copper recovery, we consider the DEP benefits of a flowchart design that can achieve a hypothetical 1% and a 5% increase in systems recovery. The findings (Fig. 2) show that if global copper production systems were able to achieve a 5% shift in the systems recovery of copper for one year and if all this increased marginal copper production were allocated to Solar/PV production, this would contribute to carbon savings of 9.89 billion tonnes over the life of the installed sustainable energy technologies. If the marginal copper were used for onshore wind technology, the potential carbon savings would be considerably higher (over 33 billion tonnes). Figure 3 visualizes the recovery-carbon trade-off across different sustainable energy technologies, illustrating the clear DEP opportunities from increasing system-level recovery alongside the DEP losses associated with lower recovery.

The cost of compromising copper recovery

The above analysis clearly illustrates the importance of optimizing recovery across copper production systems. Here, we further illustrate why it is important for mining companies to carefully design their decarbonization plans such that systems-level recovery of copper is not compromised. To do so, we modeled the acceptable systems-level recovery loss for copper production circuits, comparing it with the broader emissions savings that can be achieved by producing that additional copper for use in sustainable energy technologies. Specifically, two scenarios are modeled: (1) the percentage shift in total systems recovery losses that are acceptable based on the DEP model (Fig. 4a); and (2) the total tonnes of marginal metal the mining industry would have to deliver to create comparable carbon emissions savings from copper use within green energy technologies (Fig. 4b).

The analysis considers a theoretical scenario in which all mining companies globally design their site-level decarbonization plans to minimize CO2e emissions by adopting ore-sorting technologies, which have been estimated to reduce the total carbon emissions of a typical copper mine-to-refinery circuit by 6%9. This is achieved by using advanced sensing systems to reject undesired minerals early in the flowchart, thereby minimizing the energy required for crushing and grinding to process lower-grade material32. The technology can be classed into two broad categories: bulk-ore sorting (BOS), which incorporates sensors into materials handling equipment and allows the material to be appropriately classified as ore or waste prior to more energy-intensive downstream processes, and particle sorting, which evaluates rocks or particles individually after the crushing and grinding stages26,32

Ideally, sites would design their flowcharts to maximise the systems-level recovery of copper while minimising associated carbon emissions. Previous studies show how this can be achieved26. However, BOS can be problematic if the heterogeneity of the deposit is not suitable35 or if the sorting occurs too early in the flowchart—in such scenarios, otherwise recoverable copper may be sent to waste. It should be noted that BOS can also reclassify potential waste as ore, thereby avoiding the target mineral from being incorrectly disposed of32. Similarly with particle sorting due to the non-heterogenous nature of rocks and also the spatial location of valuable minerals in the rocks, even with the most efficient sensor, there is still a chance that valuable metal can report to the ‘reject’ stream and be sent to waste.

For the purposes of this analysis, we considered how much metal ore sorting technologies can afford to misclassify (i.e. send to waste) before any energy savings from employing these technologies are nullified due to the DEP benefits of the marginal copper that would otherwise be produced. It was assumed that, building upon IFC estimates9, the entire global mining sector could achieve a 6% reduction in emissions through adopting ore sorting as a decarbonization lever. This would result in the equivalent carbon savings of the industry deploying at least 622 tonnes/year of new marginal copper for solar technologies or 185 tonnes/year of new marginal copper is used for onshore wind. When further considering the trade-off acceptable from a systems recovery perspective for implementing ore sorting (Fig. 4a), we find that it ranges from 0.001% for onshore wind to 0.003% for offshore wind and PV. Operations in the mining industry cannot measure a reduction of 0.001–0.003% in recovery with current systems; effectively, this means that any measurable loss in system recovery across the copper production chain is unacceptable for this carbon trade-off.

Implications of DEP optimized copper production

This illustrative example of DEP has important implications for the decarbonization strategies being established by copper mining companies and underscores the need for greater alignment of incentives among the individuals and organizations involved in decision-making across the entire copper production process.

For copper mining and smelting companies, we argue that reducing their carbon footprint should remain an important goal to strive for, however this could be carefully directed towards efforts that will not result in any loss of system-level copper recovery and focus on decarbonizing efforts on projects that increase recovery. This is because, as the analysis in this paper illustrates, the benefits of marginal copper metal in aiding carbon reduction through sustainable energy technologies far outweigh the carbon emissions associated with its generation. This may lead to decisions that may appear sub-optimal from the perspective of individual stages. For example, technological solutions for reducing energy intensity in comminution could be carefully evaluated for site-specific conditions, with optimization that considers not only metallurgical recovery at Stage 2 (Fig. 1) but also prioritizes broader system-level recovery. Further downstream, there is an argument that smelters could use surplus capacity to accept lower-grade concentrate at the expense of a higher carbon footprint within their facilities, and they could show how this maximizes the system-level recovery of copper from the mine to the smelter.

Despite the argument in this paper that design choices across the entire copper production process, from the mining of the ore body through to finished metal, could be evaluated through the DEP framework as a core KPI, there are substantial social and political considerations that make this challenging in practice. First, the business model of the copper production system is fragmented, so decisions are typically made to optimize economics at the individual stages shown in Fig. 1. A change in global industry mindset would be needed among techno-economic decision-makers across the entire value chain, so they are educated around recovery as a core KPI and incentivized to change behavior to optimize the broader system. For example, geologists could establish a second cut-off grade based on DEP, resulting in less copper reporting to waste dumps. At the same time, metallurgists could adjust their grade target not only to improve recovery but also to shift grind size, potentially saving energy. Additionally, smelters would have to be flexible enough to accept lower-grade, higher-impurity concentrates. The policy environment around DEP would also need to be carefully designed such that companies are not penalized at an individual facility level for optimizing system-wide objectives.

title: Automakers are betting on a different kind of electric car. Meet the EREV. - Business Insider
description:
Several car brands, including Hyundai, Genesis, Ram, Jeep, Ford, and Volkswagen-backed Scout Motors, have announced plans to build extended-range electric vehicles, or EREVs, by the end of 2028.
An EREV has both a substantial battery and a gas engine.
Its wheels are propelled exclusively by electric motors.
The gas engine burns fuel to spin a generator, which produces electricity once the battery level falls.
But, like an EREV, its gas engine generates electricity while electric motors drive the wheels.
text:
The next popular EV might come with a gas engine.

Several car brands, including Hyundai, Genesis, Ram, Jeep, Ford, and Volkswagen-backed Scout Motors, have announced plans to build extended-range electric vehicles, or EREVs, by the end of 2028.

It's a growing industry bet. After years of lower-than-expected EV adoption, and as gas prices remain elevated, auto executives believe buyers want the experience of electric driving without having to depend on America's charging infrastructure for every long trip.

"EREVs are really the next generation of this stepping stone powertrain," Robby DeGraff, the manager of product and consumer insights at AutoPacific, told Business Insider. "These vehicles make a lot of sense for a lot of Americans."

So… what the heck is an EREV?

An EREV has both a substantial battery and a gas engine.

Its wheels are propelled exclusively by electric motors. The gas engine burns fuel to spin a generator, which produces electricity once the battery level falls.

On paper, the system combines the benefits of an EV and a gas vehicle. Owners who charge regularly can handle most daily driving on electricity, then use gasoline for long trips or heavy towing — when an all-electric truck's range can take a steep hit. Most EREVs are expected to offer roughly 120 to 150 miles of electric-only driving, followed by several hundred additional miles with a full tank of gas.

The format makes particular sense in the kinds of vehicles Americans already love: big trucks and SUVs. The fully plug-in EREVs announced so far are concentrated in those larger segments, where there is room for a substantial battery, an engine, and a fuel tank.

"Given that Americans still have an irrational desire for oversized vehicles and we'll likely continue to have elevated fuel prices for the foreseeable future, EREVs actually make a lot of sense and have the potential to do well," Sam Abuelsamid, vice president of market research at Telemetry, told Business Insider.

What's coming, and when

Automakers have not settled on a single name for the technology.

Ram's coming pickup is the clearest example. The company calls its gas-generator, electric-drive truck the Ram 1500 REV. Ram says the pickup, expected to reach dealerships in the first half of 2027, will produce 647 horsepower from electric motors, offer 145 miles of electric range, and travel up to 690 miles in total.

Its sister brand, Jeep, is preparing a related Grand Wagoneer SUV. That one is called the REEV.

Hyundai, Ford, and Scout Motors are solidly in the EREV camp. On its recent investor day, Hyundai announced that it will build a three-row Santa Fe EREV in Alabama. It's expected to launch in early 2027 with more than 600 miles of range. The company's luxury brand, Genesis, will also introduce a so-far unnamed EREV SUV.

Ford announced that its next-generation F-150 Lightning will get a gas generator after the all-electric version's sales disappointed. Finally, Scout Motors, the vintage truck brand that Volkswagen is reviving, is offering gas-generator options of its Traveler SUV and Terra pickup.

Nissan's upcoming Rogue e-POWER hybrid points in the same direction. It is not a plug-in, and Nissan does not call it an EREV. But, like an EREV, its gas engine generates electricity while electric motors drive the wheels.

They're different from other big flops

The promise of an EREV may sound familiar.

For years, car companies pitched plug-in hybrids, or PHEVs, as the best of both worlds: a battery with a plug for short trips and a gas engine for longer ones.

The category hasn't caught on.

The Energy Information Administration reported that plug-in hybrids accounted for 1.4% of US vehicle sales in the second quarter of 2026, down from 1.9% a year earlier. Stellantis announced a $26 billion write-down while discontinuing its PHEV lineup, and none of Detroit's Big Three automakers still sells a traditional plug-in hybrid in the US.

A few PHEVs have found an audience. Toyota has sold a healthy number of plug-in Priuses and RAV4s, while Mitsubishi's Outlander Plug-In Hybrid has earned strong reviews. DeGraff said he is getting 45 to 55 miles of estimated electric range from a 2026 Outlander PHEV he is currently testing.

But overall, the PHEV model has struggled at scale. The vehicles are more expensive than comparable gas cars and traditional hybrids, and their fuel-saving promise depends on owners regularly plugging them in. Studies have found that many do not.

Abuelsamid says EREVs could be a better bet for two main reasons: they're mechanically simpler, and, unlike PHEVs, the performance won't change as the car bounces between gas and electric power.

Or, EREVs could fall into the same pricing and consumer confusion traps. The Ram 1500 REV, for example, is expected to reach dealerships with pricing between $60,000 and $100,000.

"There are two massive threats to EREVs that have been damaging to today's PHEVs: cost and education," DeGraff added. "If you want a consumer to pay quite a bit more for this advanced powertrain, it is imperatively important they understand it."

title: PG&E and Rewiring America announce Google-funded virtual power plant program
description:
Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E), Rewiring America and Google have launched the Smart Home Assets for Reliability and Efficiency (SHARE) program, a virtual power plant (VPP) designed to deploy and manage flexible residential energy devices in the San Francisco Bay Area.
Rewiring America will handle customer signups and manage installer relationships, and funding for program operations and any incentives paid to participants will come from Google.
The three companies first revealed plans to provide aggregated customer-sited resources to utilities and hyperscalers in June, and the SHARE program is the first publicly-announced program to utilize that offering.
PG&E and Rewiring America say they will begin reaching out to eligible customers starting fall 2026.
The partners expect the SHARE program to run through 2027, with initial findings from the program expected to be shared in late 2026 or early 2027.
text:
Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E), Rewiring America and Google have launched the Smart Home Assets for Reliability and Efficiency (SHARE) program, a virtual power plant (VPP) designed to deploy and manage flexible residential energy devices in the San Francisco Bay Area.

In comments to pv magazine USA, PG&E and Rewiring America said they expect the SHARE program to reach approximately 12 MW of capacity by 2028, including capacity from new battery-enabled heat pumps and as many as 21,000 existing distributed energy resources like Tesla Powerwall batteries and smart home thermostats owned by PG&E customers.

Rewiring America will handle customer signups and manage installer relationships, and funding for program operations and any incentives paid to participants will come from Google.

PG&E will operate the VPP through its DERMS platform, issuing dispatch instructions and measuring performance. The utility plans to use the program to test the locational value of customer-sited resources, with both the enrollment of existing home energy devices and the regional development of privately funded new technologies structured around specific regional grid needs.

“This is about delivering power at the speed our economy demands—while improving affordability and reliability for the people we serve,” said PG&E Chief Commercial Officer Chelle Izzi in a statement. “SHARE shows how investing in customers can unlock grid capacity, support growth, and bring real benefits back to communities.”

To support the program’s operational goals, Demand Side Analytics will assist with distributed power plant orchestration, while software provider encoord will supply modeling analysis to evaluate how the VPP impacts and shapes demand on both the distribution and transmission grids.

How homeowners can participate

PG&E customers in Santa Clara and Alameda counties will be eligible to receive new high-efficiency, battery-enabled heat pumps from Carrier, with the cost of equipment and installation partially subsidized by Google. A report from Fast Company indicates that customers will receive a discount of at least $5,000 toward a heat pump installation, with $10,000 available to the first 25 households to sign up.

Eligible Bay Area homeowners with existing distributed energy resources such as home batteries and smart thermostats will be invited to join the program from a pool of customers of Sunrun, Tesla and Renew Home. The three companies first revealed plans to provide aggregated customer-sited resources to utilities and hyperscalers in June, and the SHARE program is the first publicly-announced program to utilize that offering.

PG&E says homeowners in the Sunrun/Tesla/Renew pool could receive ongoing incentives in exchange for participation (paid to customers separately from their electric bills), with the exact amount of those incentives dependent on technology, eligibility and enrollment wave.

As an example of current compensation for VPP participation, Powerwall owners enrolled under Tesla’s existing Virtual Power Plant partnership with PG&E’s Emergency Load Reduction Program (ELRP) are compensated with $2.00 for every additional kilowatt-hour (kWh) their battery delivers to the grid during a dispatched event, which can total up to $350 per year depending on the number of grid emergencies.

PG&E and Rewiring America say they will begin reaching out to eligible customers starting fall 2026. The partners expect the SHARE program to run through 2027, with initial findings from the program expected to be shared in late 2026 or early 2027.

text:
The Stockland project, delivering rooftop solar across several lifestyle villages for over-55s in Victoria, involved overcoming some major financial and technical challenges.

Working with Stockland and manufacturing partners Sungrow, the solution Venergy developed involved using the residential villages’ own fibre-optic network to coordinate how the solar panels on each home functioned.

The result was a system that could be installed at a significantly lower cost to the developer, delivering clean energy and helping residents to save over $1 million on household energy bills in its first year.

“We were talking about trenching cables under and all these different things. And it was like, well, hang on, each home has a fibre optic network that is connected – that seems so obvious. Once we got the idea, we were quite anchored to it and have basically not looked back since then.”

Partnerships powering solutions

A big part of the project’s success, Wilkins says, has been Venergy’s partnership with Sungrow.

“We go in there and it’s really nice to be part of that community, and we couldn’t really do that just with ourselves,” he says.

“We’ve got direct communication that was put together, we call it their Navy SEAL team. It’s a group of their staff that really understand how this works and we’re working on it together, hand-in-hand, really leaning on their engineering experience as well.”

With a pipeline of further work in place, Venergy is now hoping to grow its impact in the commercial solar space, supported by the federal government’s policy to extend solar PV eligibility under the Small-Scale Renewable Energy Scheme. The changes are expected to apply to eligible systems installed from October, subject to the regulations being in place, expanding eligibility for small-scale technology certificates to systems above 100kW and up to 1MW.

The certificates, known as STCs, are generally converted into an upfront reduction in the cost of the solar project, and the government has indicated this could reduce the upfront installation cost of eligible systems by around 20per cent.

For example, an eligible business could receive an upfront benefit of approximately $68,000 for a 250kW system. This could include solar power for warehouses and logistics facilities, manufacturers, commercial property, agricultural businesses, food processors and other larger energy users.

“The tide’s been out a little bit on commercial solar,” Wilkins says. “It really slowed up there for a while. I think business confidence was down just a little bit, people weren’t spending.

″⁣The market really went in hard on home batteries with that big rebate that was happening with the government, and commercial got left to the side a little bit.

″⁣I think the tide is about to come in very, very fast and we’re preparing for that.

“I think what you could say is there’s this huge gap in the market where the viability of the projects hasn’t moved forward…And now we’re going to probably see some of those businesses that are doing it for environmental targets probably double down and do even more because they’re financially able to.”

To support this growth, Venergy is embracing AI to streamline its workflow. But Wilkins says the business is also staying true to the ethos it started out with 20 years ago in country South Australia.

“Coming from a small town, you’ve got to do things right. You can’t really go to the local supermarket if you’ve done the wrong thing because there’s only one in the town, and you’re going to bump into everyone.

“Adelaide is basically just a slightly bigger version of a country town, so we’ve carried that same mentality, and it’s become a real core part of our DNA now.

“It’s not surprising that if that’s part of your business model – just doing the right thing and trying to get the best outcomes for your customers – how quickly your business can actually grow.”

text:
Infrastructure concerns

Denton is confronting a question communities across Texas will increasingly face: What happens when private development requires infrastructure on the scale of a small city?

Data centers bring investment, but being pro-business should not mean giving particular businesses special treatment.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Texas should neither ban nor subsidize data centers. Companies creating extraordinary infrastructure demands should bear the costs they create rather than shifting those risks to homeowners and small businesses.

The Legislature should protect ratepayers from stranded infrastructure costs, reconsider special data-center tax exemptions and preserve local authority over genuine local concerns such as land use, noise, water and drainage.

Texas should manage the statewide electric grid. Austin should not become Denton’s zoning board.

If a data center makes economic sense, let investors build it and let communities establish reasonable rules.

But let the people proposing the project pay their own way.

Darren Hamilton, Little Elm

Libertarian candidate for Texas House District 57

Public scrutiny necessary

As a Keller resident, I’m concerned about the rapid growth of data centers in North Texas, including the one proposed in neighboring Westlake. The issue isn’t technology or economic development; it’s the lack of transparency about their enormous demands for water and electricity.

When data center developers fail to provide reliable projections of water and energy use, municipalities can’t determine whether existing infrastructure can support them or what costly upgrades will be necessary.

Residents are then left to wonder: How much water will it use? How much electricity? Will our infrastructure handle it? And who will pay for the upgrades?

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Texas must require data centers to disclose projected water and electricity consumption, infrastructure impacts and financial responsibilities before permits are approved. That information should be public and independently verifiable so residents and local officials can make informed decisions.

Keller and Westlake deserve transparency and accountability, not development decisions made behind closed doors. If a project can’t withstand public scrutiny, it shouldn’t receive public approval.

Andrea Christgau, Keller

Crossing the line

Re: "Juror reject barratry claim — Four-day trial ended with verdict after 25 minutes of deliberation," Aug. 28 news story.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Despite the jury’s decision in this case, your reporting on barratry raises some concerning issues about vulnerable families being approached by lawyers or intermediaries while grieving after an accident.

Texas has long prohibited improper solicitation, sometimes called “ambulance chasing.” Yet, and as your story notes, the growth of social media tactics used by some lead generation intermediaries can skirt – if not cross – the line on barratry.

If third parties or other intermediaries are circumventing the law, then the Legislature should revisit our barratry statutes to address this and strengthen penalties. This kind of solicitation is not what families need in the time of tragedy.

Robert Wood, Austin

Texans Against Lawsuit Abuse

Accountability needed

Re: "Epstein files remind us justice is not blind — Too often, justice favors the well-connected," by Peter Johnson, Thursday Opinion.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Wow, just wow. Johnson nailed it. It is way past time for accountability to show its unbiased face. No accountability for Jan. 6 yet because over 1,500 arrested Capitol rioters were issued full pardons. We still have no one being held accountable.

And now, the Epstein files and no full accountability for those who were involved.

Come on, America. We can't continue to sweep these kinds of major indiscretions under the rug. This lack of holding people accountable does not meet minimum Department of Justice standards nor is it blind justice.

Jeff Foster, Carrollton

Pay attention to history

In school, we studied the Korean War. One of the main reasons North Korea was able to force us to accept a stalemate outcome was that they were solidly supported by China. China provided them with war material and funds.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

During the Vietnam catastrophe, China provided much help to North Vietnam. The result was that the United States gave up and fled the conflict.

And now, we read that China is providing a growing amount of assistance to Iran.

Regretfully, I am not sure that the Trump administration pays any attention to history or cares to learn from it.

Thomas Kelly, Lantana

Time for action

“Hundreds feared dead in devastating Nepal flood” is the latest news in what seem to be almost daily reports of severe climate events.

Climate change is increasing the likelihood and severity of many extreme weather events, underscoring the need for much stronger preventive action.

Animal agriculture is a major contributor to climate change, an existential global threat. Cattle emit large quantities of methane, a particularly potent greenhouse gas, while enormous amounts of land are devoted to grazing and growing animal feed.

Reducing consumption of animal products would enable significant reforestation. The increase in carbon-absorbing trees would reduce the current hazardous level of atmospheric carbon dioxide to a much safer level.

It’s time for action.

Dustin Erwinger, Dallas

A fan of high school football

The changing of the seasons is different in Texas. We don’t mark the beginning of fall by our leaves changing into glorious colors, or by the crisp morning air. Our trees often turn from green to brown to bare. Our mornings still hover at 80.

But we hear the sound of fall. Friday night I could hear the announcer describing the action and the band leading the charge at a neighborhood high school football game.

A good drum line brings back memories of decades of going to high school football in Texas. My parents took me as a little girl, and for years I believed the shoulder pads were real muscles. We took our children when they were small and could run around and play under the bleachers, reveling in their freedom. We had season tickets to their high school football games. As grandparents, we have come back to games.

Some things should be on everyone’s bucket list. Watching the Brownwood Lions play in Gordon Wood Stadium. Watching the Trinity Trojans' Haka dance. And preserving our public schools.

text:
It’s Monday, and that’s when we like to take a look at current business issues that are trending across our state and discuss them with one of our fellow news media friends. This week, Mike Switzer interviews Jessica Holdman, a reporter with the South Carolina Daily Gazette in Columbia, SC. Jessica tells us about a Spartanburg data center creating its own power but much more than originally projected. She also tells us about Duke Energy asking the SC Supreme Court to overturn the Public Service Commission’s ruling that Duke must wait a year before raising rates. And finally she updates us on the status of the $150 million needed to pay for cost overruns at the Scout Motors site in Blythewood, SC.

TRANSCRIPT:

Switzer: Hello and welcome to the South Carolina Business Review. This is Mike Switzer. It's Monday and that's when we like to take a look at current business issues that are trending across our state and discuss them with one of our fellow news media friends. This week we have Jessica Holdman, a reporter with the South Carolina Daily Gazette, a non profit news agency. And she joins us by phone now from her office in Columbia. Jessica, welcome back to the program.

Holdman: Thanks, Mike.

Switzer: So tell us what's showing up on your radar this week.

Holdman: Well, Mike, we've got a few headlines in the utility and power generation sphere going on. I think you and I have probably talked before about a data center in Spartanburg County. this one's being developed by Northmark Strategies and what they want to do is they want to make their own power. Now we've heard the argument against data centers that they take so much energy and it's showing up on power customers bills. Well, this company wanted to avoid that by producing their own power, but they've seen some challenges. There's been some environmental and citizens groups that are worried about air pollution from the generators they would use to do this. In this past week or so, the Public Service Commission said that actually the company's not subject to the same regulatory process as power plants are in the state. They can just go through the environmental review process.

Switzer: I guess they're not considering clean energy.

Holdman: Right. So this would be a natural gas fired turbines. Really big concern that the environmental groups raised is that when they came in they were saying, oh, we just need 50 megawatts. Then they came back and said actually it's going to be more than that. They actually upped that to needing 450 megawatts worth of generators on site. So drastic change in the amount of energy being produced certainly is. All right.

Switzer: You mentioned more in the electric, utility, sector.

Holdman: Absolutely. Duke Energy was the first utility in the state to opt to use a new mechanism that legislators passed here couple legislative sessions ago and that was setting up a process where utility companies could raise their rates on an annual basis without having to go through the full blown regulatory process. They do still have to make their argument before regulators, but it's not as long and drawn out. And when they went before the Public Service Commission, the commissioner said, well, you can do this but you're going to have to wait. They wanted the utility to have essentially a base year before they could go in and ask for a rate increase. Duke Energy is, saying that's not the way that the law was written, so they're asking the Supreme Court to step in.

Switzer: Okay, so do we know when that decision might come down?

Holdman: Well, that's really hard to say. When the court decides to take up that case remains to be seen.

Switzer: All right, Jessica, we have time for one more. What else have you found?

Holdman: One other thing we've talked about on the show in the past, Mike, is the cost overruns at the Scout Motors plant. There were some questions about whether the state would step in and cover those overruns. There was some money put in the budget with the stipulation that the money couldn't be paid out until a full blown investigation had taken place. Governor in his veto powers, stepped in and said, you know, you can have this study conducted, but we don't need to be waiting to cut that check. Most of those cost overruns were tied to environmental remediation, fixing wetlands to make up for those that were lost when the site was leveled.

Switzer: All right, so I guess this $150 million, now it's paid and the, controversy over that with Scout Motors is over.

Holdman: yeah, I mean, I'm sure we'll still see that investigation into how we got there go forward, but the question of will they or won't they has been answered.

Switzer: Well, Jessica, thank you so much for the update.

Holdman: Thanks, Mike.

Switzer: Jessica Holdman is a reporter with the South Carolina Daily Gazette. She spoke to us by phone from her office in Columbia. We will have a link to the nonprofit news source in our state posted at our webpage so you can learn more south Carolina public radio.org or you can hear this show again. And you can hear us again wherever you find podcasts with the South Carolina Business Review. This is Mike Switzer.

BARCELONA, Spain, Sept. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Smart City Expo World Congress (SCEWC), the leading international event on cities and smart urban solutions organized by Fira de Barcelona, will hold its 2026 edition from November 3 to 5 at Barcelona’s Gran Via venue, bringing together 1,000 cities, more than 25,000 attendees, over 1,000 exhibitors and 600 speakers. Under the theme “Urban Solutions, Real Impact,” this year’s edition will place special focus on housing, one of the most pressing challenges facing cities worldwide, while showcasing technologies designed to deliver tangible, scalable impact.

The congress program is structured around seven tracks — Enabling Technologies, Energy & Environment, Mobility, Governance & Economy, Living & Inclusion, Infrastructure & Building, and Blue Economy — spanning digital transformation, artificial intelligence, green energy, governance and social equity.

Over 600 experts will take part in the sessions, including Nikolas Badminton, Chief Futurist and Think Tank leader at Futurist.com, who will share his vision on the future of cities. An artificial intelligence expert, Badminton helps companies and institutions build strategic foresight capabilities, identify the trends shaping the world, anticipate unforeseen risks, and prepare for complex, evolving environments through long-term thinking and scenario planning.

Ayumi Moore Aoki, founder of Women in Tech Global, will also participate in the congress. Her work focuses on the importance of diversity and inclusion as key drivers of innovation in the urban context. Moore Aoki underscores how inclusive leadership can support sustainable urban development at scale. The conference also features Bibiana Aido of UN Women, Bilel Jamoussi of the ITU, and Chiara Corazza of the Women’s Economic Forum, among others.

SCEWC will host the first edition of HOWS Barcelona, a new housing world summit that will focus on topics such as urban planning and land policy, housing regulation, social and affordable housing, and building renovation and reuse, opening a debate on the foundations of a new residential paradigm.

The exhibition floor will host global companies including Google, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Dell Technologies and Deutsche Telekom IoT, alongside a wide range of country and city pavilions and the new “Terra50” showcase, unveiling the world’s top 50 sustainability solutions in the urban field.

SCEWC 2026 will run jointly with Tomorrow.Mobility World Congress, Tomorrow.Blue Economy, HOWS Barcelona, Barcelona Deep Tech Summit, and Barcelona Cybersecurity Congress, consolidating Barcelona as a global meeting point for urban innovation this November.
