text:
London, September 7, 2026 – South Africa’s energy system is undergoing a major transition as the nation has moved beyond the worst of its power crisis, according to BloombergNEF’s (BNEF) South Africa Transition Factbook 2026. Persistent load shedding has ended after coal power plants returned to service and private-sector participation increased.

Private clean-power procurement is becoming a defining feature of South Africa’s electricity market. In 2026, corporate power purchase agreements (PPAs) are set to drive more utility-scale renewable additions in the country than government auctions for the first time. BNEF expects corporate buyers to support 73% of the 2.3 gigawatts of anticipated solar and wind additions in 2026. Corporate buyers remain the main driver of renewables through the end of the decade.

Investors, developers and corporate energy buyers are planning further investment in clean power capacity, but transmission grid capacity is emerging as a limiting factor in how quickly these investments can go ahead. Without faster grid expansion, South Africa’s energy transition may deliver less economic growth than expected.

The rise in clean-power investment is helping to cut fossil-fuel demand, but coal is still central to South Africa’s power system, supplying 78% of electricity in 2025, down from 90% in 2015. In BNEF’s Economic Transition Scenario (ETS), which gives an economics-led view of how the power sector evolves, solar, wind and battery storage increasingly shape the country’s future. As power consumption rises by 35% to 319TWh by 2050, solar and wind expand to supply 69% of that demand, while coal falls to 21% as aging plants retire and the coal fleet shrinks.

Nelson Nsitem, Africa Research Lead at BloombergNEF, said: “South Africa’s energy transition has reached a critical inflection point. To date, private companies have played a central role in bringing new clean power into the system, but the next phase will depend on whether infrastructure can keep pace with investment. Expanding the grid and bringing down electricity costs will be critical not only to deploying more renewables, but to strengthen South Africa’s competitiveness in industries such as critical minerals and manufacturing.”

Sofia Maia, Head of Middle East and Africa Research at BloombergNEF, said: “For many South African businesses, investing in clean energy is no longer primarily a climate decision — it is increasingly about securing reliable power, managing costs and having greater control over their energy supply. That change in motivation is reshaping the country’s power market and creating a much bigger role for private investment.”

According to BNEF, South Africa is becoming increasingly reliant on China for clean-energy equipment. China accounted for 98% of solar and 95% of battery imports in 2025. In the region, China is also gaining shares in wind (80%) and electric vehicles (84%) from the US and Europe by offering lower-cost products to a price sensitive market. As sub-Saharan Africa becomes a larger market for Chinese clean-tech exports, South Africa has an opportunity to build domestic manufacturing and capture more of the region’s growing clean-energy supply chain.

Other key findings from the report include:

South Africa’s industrial decarbonization is becoming a competitiveness issue, not just an emissions issue, as policies such as the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) increase pressure on emissions-intensive exports. South Africa’s industrial base is concentrated in energy-intensive mining and metals production, making these sectors central to the country’s decarbonization challenge. Coal’s dominant role in final energy demand highlights the potential for fuel switching and electrification to reduce industrial emissions.

South Africa has a strategic edge in energy-transition supply chains as a major supplier of strategic minerals, such as platinum-group metals, manganese and chrome. Despite the opportunity, the nation captures relatively little value downstream as high power costs and infrastructure constraints weigh on competitiveness. High power prices are hampering the government’s ambition to grow its critical minerals industry, with average industrial electricity prices sitting at R1,652/MWh last year compared to R964/MWh in mainland China.

South Africa’s EV strategy could revive its auto competitiveness. EV sales more than doubled in 2025, although they still accounted for 1% of the total South African passenger vehicle market. The sector is receiving incentives to produce EVs, for both the local and export markets, through measures including the enhanced Automotive Investment Scheme (AIS) and a 150% first-year tax deduction on investments in zero-emission vehicle manufacturing from March 2026. Shifting existing auto manufacturing capacity toward EVs could support South Africa’s export competitiveness as major overseas markets transition away from internal-combustion engines.

South Africa remains the largest market in sub-Saharan Africa renewable energy investment at $5.4 billion in 2025. South Africa’s renewable energy investment fell 41% from $8.6 billion in 2024. Fewer utility-scale projects reached financial close in 2025, with utility solar down 57% to $1.4 billion, and onshore wind dropping 30% to $2.1 billion. Small-scale solar broke the trend, growing 35% to $1.8 billion and softening the overall drop.

The South Africa Transition Factbook 2026 examines how the country’s key sectors are affected by the energy transition, where new opportunities and risks are emerging, and how mineral resources, local manufacturing and further policy reforms could shape competitiveness and long-term growth.

title: Best Large SUVs 2026 – Electric - WhichCar
description:
While there are both newer and cheaper large electric SUVs on offer, the iX remains one of the most complete.
The 2026 BMW iX isn’t the cheapest electric large SUV on sale, but that doesn’t mean that it’s not worth a look.
It’s definitely the sportiest contender in the electric section of the Wheels Best Large SUV 2026, so how does it fare against its competition?
The Polestar 3 is also quite a practical large SUV, with ample space for five on offer.
For buyers seeking an electric large SUV that is as rewarding to drive as it is to live with, the Polestar 3 is deserving of serious attention.
text:
Contenders

Volvo EX90

BMW iX

Hyundai Ioniq 9

Kia EV9

Mercedes-Benz G580 with EQ Technology

Polestar 3

Winner: Volvo EX90

Price: From $106,990 plus on-road costs

Drivetrain: Single- or dual-motor electric, rear- or all-wheel drive, single-speed transmission,

92kWh or 106kWh batteries

Outputs: 245kW/480Nm (Plus) or 500kW/870Nm (Ultra)

Claimed range: 479km (Plus) – 521km (Ultra)

Warranty: Five-year/unlimited km (car), eight year/160,000km (EV battery)

Five-year service cost: Included in the price

Winning Wheels Best Large SUV – Electric 2026 takes more than impressive performance figures or the longest driving range. It requires excellence across the ownership experience, and we think that’s precisely where the Volvo EX90 separates itself from the field.

Combining a genuinely luxurious interior, outstanding safety features, adult seven-seat practicality and EV tech, the EX90 is a complete package.

The dedicated EV platform provides an expansive cabin with room for seven adults, while the long 2985mm wheelbase creates impressive second- and third-row accommodation that’s genuinely usable for even taller passengers. Families will also appreciate the generous luggage capacity of between 384L with the third row erected and a huge 2135L with all rear seats folded. The seats also fold flat, which is perfect for trips to Ikea for flatpack furniture.

The cabin itself is among the most luxurious and high quality in the segment. Volvo has embraced its usual Scandinavian minimalism, but the EX90 remains welcoming and intuitive. Beautifully finished materials, very comfortable seats and exceptional build quality create an atmosphere that’s luxurious, but in typical Volvo fashion, it’s not flashy or over the top.

A large 14.5-inch touchscreen uses Google’s Android Automotive operating system and integrates Google Maps navigation and connected services, as well as over-the-air software updates that genuinely improve the EX90 throughout its life.

As you’d expect for a Volvo, the EX90’s driver assistance technologies are impressive, including its Pilot Assist functionality, which combines adaptive cruise control, adaptive lane guidance and even driver-activated automatic lane changing to greatly assist highway driving.

On the road, that relaxed character continues. Rather than chasing sportiness – that’s what its Polestar 3 platform mate is for – the EX90 focuses on comfort and refinement, delivering a quiet and composed driving experience.

New for the 2027 model year is an entry-level Plus model, which has introduced a rear-wheel drive setup to the EX90 for the first time in Australia. Making 245kW/480Nm outputs, it’s got more than enough grunt for most, but importantly, has reduced the EX90’s entry price to $106,990 plus on-road costs – around the same or less than its biggest rivals like the Kia EV9 and Hyundai Ioniq 9, both of which don’t feel as luxurious inside. The flagship Twin Motor Ultra ($134,990 +ORC) makes huge 500kW/870Nm outputs, enough to propel it from 0-100km/h in just 4.9 seconds.

Like the Polestar 3, the EX90 was also recently updated with an 800V architecture, and that has also upgraded its DC fast charging capability to up to 350kW for a 10-80 per cent charge in as little as 22 minutes. Its 92kWh and 106kWh batteries give a WLTP-rated range of up to 521km, which is less than before, but its faster charging capability is more convenient for owners.

Ultimately, the Volvo EX90 wins here because it delivers more than just an excellent electric drivetrain. It’s beautifully built, quite practical, supremely comfortable and packed with useful technology.

BMW iX

Price: From $142,900 plus on-road costs

Drivetrain: Dual-motor electric, all-wheel drive, single-speed transmission, 94.8kWh battery

Outputs: 300kW/700Nm

Claimed range: 602km (WLTP)

Warranty: Five-year/unlimited km

Six-year service cost: $3610

Upon its release in 2021, the pre-updated BMW iX was certainly a big statement from the brand. EVs weren’t as prevalent as they are now, and the iX’s styling was divisive. But with its mid-life update, the iX has matured into a convincing large electric SUV as it combines strong performance, a long-distance claimed driving range and a very premium cabin. While there are both newer and cheaper large electric SUVs on offer, the iX remains one of the most complete.

Pricing starts from around $142,900 plus on-road costs for the single xDrive 45 model available in Australia, which places it firmly in the premium end of the segment, but the iX justifies that positioning with the depth of its engineering and polish.

Power comes from a dual-motor, all-wheel-drive electric drivetrain producing 300kW and 700Nm, which gives enough grunt for a brisk 0-100km/h time of just 5.1 seconds. But it’s also just very smooth in the way it unleashes its oomph, and its adaptive suspension gives it a strong level of composure. It feels secure and planted on the highway, yet because it’s a BMW, remains surprisingly agile through corners for such a substantial SUV.

Equally impressive is its battery and charging capability. A usable 94.8kWh battery provides a claimed driving range of up to 602km (WLTP), making long-distance touring genuinely achievable without constant charging stops. When it is time to recharge, DC fast charging at up to 175kW allows a 10-80 per cent top-up charge in under 34 minutes, which is healthy in this market.

Inside, the iX continues to set a high standard for modern luxury. The minimalist dashboard is dominated by BMW’s curved digital display, while premium materials, excellent build quality and supportive and endlessly adjustable front seating create an environment that feels expensive.

Despite its futuristic appearance, the cabin features are intuitive to use as the touchscreen can also be controlled by the familiar iDrive controller and some physical buttons for shortcuts.

Practicality in the iX is strong as well. Its flat-floor electric platform offers generous accommodation for five adults, while the 500-litre boot expands to a huge 1750 litres with the rear seats folded, though there is no front boot, annoyingly. There’s also a lot of storage throughout the cabin, along with an airy feel created by the big windows and panoramic glass roof.

The 2026 BMW iX isn’t the cheapest electric large SUV on sale, but that doesn’t mean that it’s not worth a look. Instead, it excels in offering a strong balance of luxury, refinement, performance, practicality and long-range usability. For buyers wanting a luxury electric SUV that feels as accomplished on a cross-country road trip as it does on the daily commute, the iX remains a strong contender.

Hyundai Ioniq 9

Price: From $119,750 plus on-road costs

Drivetrain: Dual-motor electric, all-wheel drive, single-speed transmission, 110.3kWh battery

Outputs: 314kW/700Nm

Claimed range: 600km (WLTP)

Warranty: Five-year/unlimited km (car) extendable to seven years with dealer servicing, eight-

year/160,000km (EV battery)

Five-year service cost: $1365

Hyundai’s electric vehicles have really helped its sales success globally, and its Ioniq 9 is the largest of the bunch. As the brand’s flagship electric SUV, it combines genuine seven-seat practicality with an impressive driving range for such a large vehicle, ultra-fast charging and a thoughtfully designed cabin that feels every bit as modern as its futuristic styling suggests. More importantly for consumers, it delivers all of that at a price that undercuts many European rivals, making it a standout contender.

Unlike some electric SUVs that simply replace an existing combustion model, the Ioniq 9 has been designed from the outset as an EV. Built on Hyundai’s dedicated ‘E-GMP’ platform, its very long 3130mm wheelbase has created exceptional interior space, allowing all three seating rows to comfortably accommodate adults. Even with every seat in use, there’s still enough luggage room for a family getaway (338 litres with all seats up and 908 litres with the third row folded), while folding the rear seats gives the Ioniq 9 a huge loading space (2419L). But there are also multiple clever storage solutions in the front cabin.

That spaciousness is matched by an interior that looks genuinely premium, and feels it in most places as well, though we think the cheaper hybrid Palisade feels even more expensive inside. Twin 12.3-inch displays feature on the dashboard, while high-quality materials, comfortable seating and Hyundai’s ergonomic layout make it an easy vehicle to live with every day. Unlike some rivals, Hyundai has thankfully retained physical controls, making the Ioniq 9 simple to operate despite its long list of features.

Australian pricing for the Ioniq 9 starts at $119,750 plus on-road costs for the Calligraphy model, which is the only model on offer locally for now, with no cheaper entry-level spec available. While it’s obviously not cheap, it is very well equipped, with major features including 21-inch alloy wheels, 14-speaker Bose audio, Nappa leather upholstery, heated and ventilated front- and middle-row seating, a panoramic glass roof and a long list of active safety features, including very effective blind-spot cameras.

Performance is strong in the Ioniq 9 as its twin-motor drivetrain produces up to 315kW of power and 700Nm of torque, which provides swift performance. More impressive than outright speed, however, is the refinement. The drivetrain is smooth, road and wind noise are well suppressed, and the suspension delivers a comfortable ride despite the 21-inch standard wheels.

Every Ioniq 9 in Australia features a large 110.3kWh battery, delivering a claimed driving range of up to 600km (WLTP) depending on the variant. The brand’s proven 800-volt electrical architecture also remains a big advantage as it can DC fast charge at up to 350kW for a claimed 10 to 80 per cent recharge in as little as 24 minutes.

As we’ve seen with most of Hyundai’s current lineup, the Ioniq 9 is an excellent all-rounder that will win fans based on just how much it can do, such as its huge cabin space that can accommodate up to seven adults, its long list of standard features, comfortable driving experience and cheap service costs. In this case, it also just happens to be electric, with a lot of performance, a long range and quick fast charging on offer. We think it’s a force to be reckoned with.

Kia EV9

Price: From $97,000 plus on-road costs

Drivetrain: Single- or dual-motor electric, rear- or all-wheel drive, single-speed transmission,

76.1kWh or 99.8kWh batteries

Outputs: 160kW/350Nm (Air), 282kW/700Nm (Earth and GT-Line), 374kW/740Nm (GT)

Claimed range: 443km (Air), 512km (Earth), 505km (GT-Line), 510km (GT)

Warranty: Seven-year/unlimited km (car), seven-year/150,000km (EV battery)

Five-year service cost: $1379

The Kia EV9 arrived in Australia in late 2023 to much surprise. It landed as one of the first genuinely practical seven-seat EVs, and even as rivals have steadily joined the segment, the EV9 continues to impress with its combination of space, technology, refinement and everyday usability.

Rather than simply offering an electric alternative to a large SUV, the EV9 was designed from the ground up to meet the needs of modern families, and that’s why we think it’s a great product. One of the EV9’s greatest strengths is value. While it’s certainly not what you’d call cheap, and remains the most expensive Kia ever sold, it offers a lot of standard equipment.

Australian pricing begins at around $97,000 plus on-road costs for the Air, rising to just over $129,250 +ORC for the flagship GT. Across the range, standard features are generous, such as dual 12.3-inch displays, wireless smartphone connectivity, heated seats and a comprehensive suite of active safety systems. Move up the range to the GT and 21-inch wheels, racy lime-green details and camera side mirrors feature as standard.

Practicality has always been at the heart of the EV9, and it remains one of the most accommodating electric SUVs on sale. Its dedicated ‘E-GMP’ platform – yep, the same one underneath the Ioniq 9 – features a long wheelbase and completely flat floor, resulting in a spacious cabin with room for seven occupants. The EV9’s rear seats are genuinely usable by adults, too – even for longer trips.

There’s also ample luggage capacity ranging up to 2393 litres, while thoughtful touches such as numerous storage compartments, USB-C charging points and air vents throughout the cabin make life easier.

The powertrain options for the EV9 range also give buyers plenty of choice. The entry-level Air is available with either a rear-wheel-drive single-motor setup, while the Earth, GT-Line and GT come exclusively with all-wheel drive. The GT makes 374kW/7040Nm outputs, resulting in rapid acceleration despite the EV9’s considerable size – it hits 100km/h in just 4.5 seconds and a top speed of 200km/h.

Thanks to its local tuning program, Kia has struck an excellent balance between ride comfort and body control, making the EV9 equally at home around town or on highways.

Australian EV9 variants use either a 76.1kWh (Air) or 99.8kWh (Earth, GT-Line and GT) battery, delivering a claimed WLTP driving range of up to 512km. Thanks to its advanced 800-volt architecture, the EV9 can accept DC fast charging at up to 350kW, allowing a 10 to 80 per cent recharge in around 24 minutes under ideal conditions.

The cabin is another highlight with its clean, contemporary design combining sustainable materials with impressive build quality, though it could do with a bit more character. A trio of displays (two 12.3-inch units and a smaller 5.0-inch display for the climate control) gives the dashboard a modern appearance without becoming overwhelming, while the infotainment system also features physical controls for key climate and audio functions. We wish more manufacturers featured cabin layouts like the EV9 because it’s quite easy to use.

As we’ve seen with a plethora of modern Kia products, the EV9 stands out because it gets so much correct and is an excellent large SUV that just happens to be electric. It offers genuine seven-seat practicality, long-range capability, rapid charging, impressive refinement and an extensive list of standard equipment, all wrapped in a bold, distinctive design. For families ready to embrace electric motoring without compromising on space or versatility, it’s easy to understand why the EV9 remains one of the benchmark options on the market.

Mercedes-Benz G 580 with EQ Technology

Price: From $252,700 plus on-road costs

Drivetrain: Dual-motor electric, four-wheel drive, two-speed transmission, 116kWh battery

Outputs: 432kW/1164Nm

Claimed range: 473km (WLTP)

Warranty: Five-year/unlimited km (car), eight-year/160,000km (EV battery)

Five-year service cost: $4670

As one of the most iconic cars still sold today, the Mercedes-Benz G-Class has built its reputation over more than 40 years as one of the world’s most capable off-road vehicles. Turning that icon into an electric vehicle was a bold move, yet the G 580 with EQ Technology proves the legendary G Wagen can embrace electrification without sacrificing its character. It remains immensely capable off the beaten track, but now adds near-silent thrust, strong performance and healthy charging statistics to the equation.

Unlike most electric SUVs, the G 580 isn’t trying to be futuristic – instead, it’s unapologetically a G-Class, with its exposed door hinges, flat body panels and upright windscreen carried over from the ICE models. Inside, the G 580’s cabin is almost identical to other G Wagen models, aside from a few EQ menus and some switchgear. Therefore, it still features high-quality materials and switchgear, as well as the same user-friendly MBUX infotainment system.

Its electric drivetrain is unlike anything else in the segment. Rather than using one or two motors, the G 580 employs four individually controlled electric motors – that’s one for each wheel – producing 432kW of power and an enormous 1164Nm of torque. That gives the G 580 excellent performance – it hits 100km/h in just 4.7 seconds, or 0.3 seconds lower than the twin-turbo V8 AMG G 63 – but also fantastic off-road ability, as you’d expect for a G Wagen. Its torque can be directed to individual wheels, while features such as ‘G-Turn’ allow the G 580 to spin on the spot on loose surfaces.

Its on- and off-road capabilities are powered by a huge 116kWh lithium-ion battery integrated into the ladder-frame chassis. Mercedes-Benz claims a WLTP driving range of up to 473km, which is longer than you might expect for such a big, boxy and heavy car. When it’s time to recharge, DC fast charging at up to 200kW allows a 10 to 80 per cent top-up in as little as 32 minutes, while 11kW AC charging is reasonable, but higher 22kW AC charging is optionally available as well.

Practicality has never been the G-Class’s primary selling point, yet the G 580 is still a usable large SUV. Don’t expect the same level of space compared to other Mercedes-Benz SUVs, however. Four adults will be able to travel in comfort thanks to its upright seating position and generous headroom, though its packaging means that rear legroom isn’t plentiful, but the 620 litre (rear seats up)/1990 litre (rear seats folded) boot offers ample cargo capacity.

Of course, the G 580’s all-round ability comes at a price. Sitting at the top of the luxury SUV market, Australian pricing starts at $252,700 before on-road costs and before any options. That positions it well beyond the more mainstream electric SUVs it’s competing with here, but few vehicles on the market offer the same blend of luxury, strong engineering and genuine off-road capability.

All things considered, the Mercedes-Benz G 580 isn’t the cheapest, most practical or most modern-feeling vehicle, but it is excellent. There were skeptics when the brand announced plans to turn one of the world’s most iconic off-roaders electric, but thanks to its awesome four-motor drivetrain giving both stonking performance and great off-road ability, a huge battery for a surprisingly long range and healthy charging statistics up to 200kW, the G 580 has proven the naysayers wrong. For them, the petrol AMG G 63 and diesel G 450d are still the go-to variants, but for the well-heeled seeking a brilliant all-round electric large SUV, the G 580 is a great choice.

Polestar 3

Price: From $116,700 plus on-road costs

Drivetrain: Single- or dual-motor electric, rear- or all-wheel drive, single-speed transmission,

92kWh or 106kWh batteries

Outputs: 245kW/480Nm (Rear Motor Plus), 400kW/740Nm (Dual Motor Plus), 500kW/870Nm

(Performance)

Claimed range: 604km (Rear Motor Plus), 647km (Dual Motor Plus), 601km (Performance) (all

WLTP)

Warranty: Five-year/unlimited km (car), eight-year/160,000km (EV battery)

Five-year service cost: Included in the price of the car

Volvo’s former offshoot brand Polestar continues to slowly build up its Australian sales with new products, and a heavily updated version of its 3 large SUV is the latest to hit our market. While it doesn’t appear it from the outside, the 3 now sits on an 800V platform for much faster charging, as well as bringing a new range of batteries and outputs. It’s definitely the sportiest contender in the electric section of the Wheels Best Large SUV 2026, so how does it fare against its competition?

Unlike many rivals that lean heavily on oversized screens or extravagant styling, the Polestar 3 adopts a more restrained Scandinavian approach, which we quite like. The exterior is clean and handsome, while the cabin uses the minimalist design language that we’ve become used to from the brand. High-quality recycled and sustainably sourced materials feature throughout, the fit and finish are excellent, and the driving position is great as well. The Polestar 3 feels luxurious without being over the top, and its cabin is warm and calming.

Performance is another of the Polestar 3’s strongest assets. Australian buyers can choose between the Single Motor, Dual Motor or Performance models, with the former rear-driven and the latter two both all-wheel drive. Even the entry-level Single Motor model makes 245kW/480Nm outputs, which are good enough for a 6.5-second 0-100km/h time, but move up to the Performance and it makes a huge 500kW and 870Nm, with a claimed 3.9-second 0-100km/h time. Yet despite those outputs, the 3 never feels overwhelmingly fast.

In this company, its driving experience is equally impressive. Adaptive air suspension features on the Dual Motor and Performance, giving it a strong level of composure for enthusiastic motoring, but crucially, it doesn’t compromise on comfort. There’s a sense of connection through the steering that many rival SUVs struggle to achieve, reinforcing Polestar’s focus on delivering a rewarding driver’s car rather than simply another premium EV.

Part of the 3’s recent update includes a revised range of batteries with either 92kWh or 106kWh units now available. They’re actually smaller than before, and give it a WLTP range of up to 647km in the Dual Motor Plus variant. That’s less than the previous 706km maximum, but thanks to the new 800V architecture, it can now charge 100kW faster at up to a 350kW maximum (310kW in the Single Motor) for a claimed 10-80 per cent charge time of as little as 22 minutes, or 25 per cent faster than before.

The Polestar 3 is also quite a practical large SUV, with ample space for five on offer. The long 2985mm long wheelbase has plenty of rear space for adults, with particularly impressive rear-seat legroom and a completely flat floor. The reasonable 484-litre boot (1411L with the rear seats folded) is joined by a useful 32-litre front boot for storing charging cables and other equipment.

Inside, the vertical 14.5-inch touchscreen runs Google’s native Android Automotive operating system, offering built-in Google Maps, Google Assistant and access to a growing range of apps without relying on smartphone mirroring, though Apple CarPlay is also along for the ride for those who want it. A stunning 1610-watt 25-speaker Bowers & Wilkins sound system is now standard across the range too.

The Polestar 3 is not cheap, starting from $116,700 plus on-road costs, but it arrives quite well equipped and the former $9000 Plus Pack (with features such as a head-up display, noise cancellation tech, an electric steering column and acoustic class) is now standard. The five-year/unlimited km warranty package also includes servicing for the first five years.

The updated Polestar 3 doesn’t attempt to reinvent the large electric SUV formula, but it’s now a much better car than it used to be and quite compelling in the segment. With a long range, now-faster charging, an engaging driving experience, strong practicality and a cabin of high quality, it’s a very complete product. For buyers seeking an electric large SUV that is as rewarding to drive as it is to live with, the Polestar 3 is deserving of serious attention.

text:
The war on EVs is far from over, but signs of electrification victory are already emerging as the war in Iran continues to push the cost of fuel through the roof. The latest examples come from the politically blue East Coast states of New York and New Jersey along with the similarly blue West Coast states of California, Oregon, and Washington, where plans are in the works to stimulate more activity in the electric truck field.

Electric Trucks Save Big Bucks

In a last-ditch effort to distract the public from his war in Iran, the Epstein files, and a growing list of grifty corruption scandals, US President Donald Trump has finally decided to…change his hair. True fact. Over the Labor Day weekend, the President transitioned from Beach Boy Blonde to Fred Trump Brown. That distracted the media to some extent, but one bottle of Nice ‘n’ Easy won’t push down the price of diesel, which hit a record high of $5.85 per gallon on September 4 according to the AAA gas price tracker.

Against this backdrop, stakeholders in the electric truck field are licking their chops. Back in 2021, when diesel prices spiked during the COVID crisis, the University of California-Berkeley ran the numbers and came up with a figure of 13% savings to run a long haul electric truck compared to diesel, with a drop in the cost of batteries contributing to a lifetime savings of up to $200,000.

UC Berkeley also anticipated a 50% savings by 2030, which is just around the corner. Whether or not that forecast proves true remains to be seen, but in the meantime the International Council on Clean Transportation has developed a meticulously calibrated total cost of ownership calculator, which enables EV-curious fleet managers and operators to see for themselves. The ICCT TCO calculator covers commercial vehicles from Class 2b–3 medium-duty delivery vans and the like, to Class 8 long-haul trucks.

That’s all well and good, but a solid network of truck-friendly EV charging stations is needed to help get fleet managers and owner-operators get over the heebie-jeebies of switching from diesel to electric, and that’s where the East and West coasts have swung into action.

$451 Million From The US EPA Clean Ports Program…Wait, What?

On the East Coast side, the latest news involves a $451 million grant issued in 2024 from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, which operates the busiest container seaport on the East Coast. The Port Authority oversees facilities shared between New York and New Jersey on both sides of the Hudson River, including bridges, tunnels, and transit assets such as the beloved PATH train and the Midtown Bus Terminal.

The 2024 grant was a carve-out from the 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law through EPA’s Clean Ports program, aimed at accelerating the transition to low- and zero-emission trucks, ships, and cargo equipment at the container ports.

Somehow that grant survived the Trump chopper. If you can figure out how that came to be, you deserve a medal and please share your insights in the discussion thread.

Regardless of how and why the funding remains intact, on September 3, 2026, the Port Authority announced that $45 million from the Clean Ports pot has been earmarked for a partnership with the nonprofit electrification organization CALSTART, aimed at kicking up the adoption of electric trucks and other electrified equipment at Port Authority facilities.

At $39 million, the bulk of the CALSTART partnership goes to support the purchase of zero-emission trucks, yard tractors and on-site supporting infrastructure. The remaining $5 million is slated for up to five off-site electric truck charging hubs, to be located within 10 miles of a Port Authority seaport or marine terminal.

Starting now-ish, staff from the Port Authority and CALSTART will begin reaching out to stakeholders in the trucking business to solicit interest. Not leaving everything up to digital communications, the outreach will include in-person presentations.

CALSTART is also tasked with developing dashboards to track the progress of both programs. “These tools will monitor deployment, vehicle performance, and charger utilization across port operations before being fully transferred to the Port Authority in 2028,” the Port Authority explains.

That’s just for starters. The Port Authority also notes that the Clean Ports grant covers other programs beyond the CALSTART partnership, including funds for electrifying cargo equipment at marine terminals, and zero emission plug-in stations that enable vessels at berth to shut down their auxiliary engines.

“A separate $3 million EPA planning grant will fund the creation of a Port Community Advisory Council,” the Port Authority adds, with the aim of improving clean energy workforce training and job opportunities in the region.

Meanwhile, The US, Canada, And Mexico…What?

The Port Authority’s EV-friendly announcement is larded with sustainability references, amounting to a Port Authority-sized poke in the eye of Trump and his Republican allies in Congress, who collaborated to prematurely kill the all-important federal EV tax credit last year.

Another, even bigger poke is coming from California, Oregon, and Washington State, all three of which have embraced Trump’s #1 and #2 enemies — Canada and Mexico — to support a new electric truck transportation corridor program.

On August 26, elected officials from the three West Coast states joined with officials from British Columbia in Canada and Baja California in Mexico to announce the new “BC2BC” (British Columbia to Baja California) ZEV corridor on Interstate-5, enabling electric trucks to travel from one end to the other with the assurance of charging station availability all along the way.

“Once completed, freight shippers and operators will be able to charge their zero-emissions fleets along the entire West Coast with the initial buildout including 20 electric charging stations and 3 hydrogen stations,” the BC2BC program elaborates.

There’s plenty more where that came from. According to BC2BC, truck traffic on the I-5 corrider currently averages 10,000 vehicles per day. Twenty EV charging stations and three hydrogen stations (for fuel cell electric trucks) is a healthy start, but many more will be needed once the I-5 is saturated with electric trucks, which it will be if all goes according to plan.

Tesla, for one, is in there pitching with the new Class 8 Semi long haul truck. Now in volume production to positive reviews, the Semi is giving Tesla some breathing room between the Cybertruck flop and the underwhelming (and questionable) Cybercab rollout in Texas last week.

Among other stakeholders, keep an eye on ZM Trucks, the US branch of Japan’s ZO Motors (an arm of the Hong Kong conglomerate ZO Future Group). In 2024 ZM Trucks announced plans to manufacture both battery electric and fuel cell electric trucks in the US with a concentration on “Baby 8” trucks as well as Classes 4-6, and Class 8. The plans were still in place after Trump took office last year.

ZM’s press room has been rather quiet since August of 2025, when the company announced its new headquarters and factory in the city of Fontana, California. However, the company exhibited proof of life at the official BC2BC launch event at the Port of Long Beach, which featured one of it trucks alongside Tesla and Volvo.

As a further poke at Trump’s psychotic isolationism, BC2BC is part of the global Drive to Zero commercial vehicle electrification initiative, supported in the US by CALSTART, which seems to be rather busy these days. In addition to CALSTART/Drive to Zero, other partners in BC2BC are the Institute of Transportation Studies at the University of California, Davis, and the California State Transportation Agency.

text:
September 7, 2026

SEOUL – Hyundai Motor Group Executive Chair Chung Euisun stood beside US President Donald Trump at the White House 17 months ago to unveil one of the Korean auto giant’s biggest bets on American manufacturing.

At the heart of the $21 billion US investment package unveiled in March 2025 — later increased to $26 billion — was a $5.8 billion steel mill in Louisiana, the group’s first steel production base in the US and a move to make one of the most essential materials for vehicles directly on US soil.

On Friday, that pledge looked very different from the polished Roosevelt Room in Washington. Rain had swept across southern Louisiana earlier in the day, but by afternoon clouds had cleared and the sun beat down on sugarcane fields stretching along the roads into Donaldsonville, a small city in in Ascension Parish with a long history of sugarcane farming.

Much of the 7.37 square-kilometer site, once sugarcane farmland, had been graded for the major work ahead. A handful of excavators, bulldozers and dump trucks dotted the vast property alongside temporary buildings serving as site offices.

There is no steel mill here yet. Full-scale construction is set to begin in the fourth quarter once permitting procedures are cleared.

But by 2029, Hyundai Steel, the steel making unit of Hyundai Motor Group, expects the empty land to be transformed into an integrated steelmaking complex capable of producing 2.7 million tons of steel annually to be used for vehicle bodies.

It was here Friday that Hyundai Steel and Posco, South Korea’s two largest steelmakers and longtime competitors at home, formally marked the launch of Hyundai-Posco Louisiana Steel, or HPLS, their first joint electric arc furnace steelmaking venture in the US.

More than 250 senior government officials from the US and South Korea, as well as business leaders, gathered to celebrate the project’s first tangible milestone since its announcement last March.

“This plant will be both our company’s first integrated steel mill dedicated to automotive steel sheet and the first of its kind in America,” Chung said at the groundbreaking ceremony. “The steel produced here will support Hyundai Motor Group and other automakers as they build the next generation of mobility.”

Made in America

The ceremony carried a wider message that went beyond the steel mill itself. It highlighted deepening industrial ties between South Korea and the US and a renewed push to manufacture more goods and materials used in America on American soil.

“As America strengthens its manufacturing leadership, steel will continue to power the next chapter of its industrial resurgence,” said Chung. “We are proud to contribute to that vision and to the future of ‘Made in America.’”

US officials echoed that message, holding up the Louisiana project as a model for the type of investment Washington wants from foreign manufacturers: not simply assembling finished products in the US, but building the entire supply chain behind them.

“Reshoring is not just about final assembly,” said William Kimmitt, Under Secretary of Commerce for International Trade. “We want the steel here. We want the parts here. We want the suppliers here. We want the technology, the investment and the jobs here. We want the entire industrial ecosystem here in the US.”

For Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry, the project was also about bringing manufacturing jobs back to the region.

“Under President Trump’s ‘America First’ agenda, we are reshoring that manufacturing here in America,” said Larry. “That means great-paying jobs right here in America, but more importantly in Louisiana.”

The project is expected to have a significant economic impact on the region. Once the mill is up and running, the project is expected to create 1,300 direct jobs and 4,100 indirect jobs, according to the company.

Deepening US-Korea industrial ties

South Korean officials, meanwhile, framed HPLS as an example of how the two countries can combine their respective industrial strengths.

“America has energy, a skilled workforce and a great market. Korea has manufacturing strength and decades of industrial experience,” Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said. “Together, we can build more. Together, we can create more jobs and together, we can compete better.”

Speaking to reporters after the ceremony, Kim called the project a “win-win” for all sides.

“Hyundai and Posco gain a new opportunity, while the US gets the steel mill it wants,” Kim said.

He added that projects like HPLS could move the two countries beyond conventional cooperation toward a broader partnership, opening opportunities not only in the US but in global markets.

Rivals unite in America

The project has also brought together two longtime rivals in South Korea’s steel industry.

Hyundai Steel and Posco have spent decades competing for automotive steel customers at home. In Louisiana, they will be shareholders in the same mill.

Hyundai Steel holds a 50 percent stake in HPLS, Posco 20 percent, while Hyundai Motor and Kia each hold 15 percent.

“Posco and Hyundai Steel may be competitors domestically, but globally, we are both Korean companies,” Posco Group Chair Chang In-hwa told reporters after the ceremony. “By working together overseas, we can strengthen the presence and competitiveness of Korean companies in the global market.”

Chang said by leveraging Posco’s extensive customer in the US, the steel produced at HPLS to pursue businesses not only with Hyundai Motor Group but also to other carmakers, including General Motors, Ford and Stellantis.

The British Business Bank has agreed to commit up to £46 million to Zinc Capital Management’s Science-for-Impact Fund, providing a cornerstone investment for the early-stage venture fund focused on UK deep tech companies addressing health and environmental challenges.
The commitment is being made through the British Business Bank’s Enterprise Capital Funds program and follows the Bank’s previous investment in Zinc II in 2022.

text:
The British Business Bank has agreed to commit up to £46 million to Zinc Capital Management’s Science-for-Impact Fund, providing a cornerstone investment for the early-stage venture fund focused on UK deep tech companies addressing health and environmental challenges.

The commitment is being made through the British Business Bank’s Enterprise Capital Funds program and follows the Bank’s previous investment in Zinc II in 2022.

Zinc’s Science-for-Impact Fund is targeting a £70 million fund size and plans to build a portfolio of approximately 80 new deep tech companies.

The strategy will focus on founders developing science-led businesses across areas aligned with the U.K. government’s Industrial Strategy priorities, including advanced manufacturing, clean energy and life sciences, along with technologies spanning engineering, biology and artificial intelligence.

Zinc is an early-stage venture capital investor and venture builder that works with founders at the earliest stages of company creation, when access to institutional funding can be especially limited.

The firm’s model combines initial capital with hands-on venture-building support intended to help founders validate scientific concepts, establish commercial strategies and develop their companies into investment-ready businesses.

The new British Business Bank commitment is intended to help Zinc expand that model and support a larger number of science-led startups across the U.K.

As a cornerstone investor, the British Business Bank can help venture funds reach an initial close while providing additional validation that may support fundraising from private-sector investors.

The Bank said its broader Enterprise Capital Funds program is designed to increase the availability of equity capital for early-stage U.K. businesses with long-term growth potential while reducing barriers for venture capital managers entering or expanding within the market.

The Zinc Science-for-Impact Fund becomes the 55th Enterprise Capital Fund supported through the program.

Zinc’s existing portfolio includes companies developing technologies across medicine, healthcare and the energy transition.

Portfolio companies include SignaCor, which is developing therapeutics for heart disease; Epiome, an AI-powered biomarker platform for neurodegenerative diseases; Speek, a digital clinical care platform addressing teenage self-harm; Spine, an AI operating system for grid-scale battery asset management; and CellMine, which is developing a waste-free process for recycling lithium-ion batteries.

The fund’s investment strategy is centered on turning scientific breakthroughs into scalable companies capable of generating both commercial returns and measurable societal impact.

Zinc plans to invest from the earliest stages and work closely with management teams as they move from scientific development toward commercialization and larger institutional funding rounds.

The British Business Bank is the U.K. government’s economic development bank and is one of the largest investors in domestic venture and venture growth funds.

During the 2025/26 financial year, the Bank supported U.K. smaller businesses in accessing approximately £9.4 billion of finance, consisting of £1.3 billion in public funding, £4.3 billion of private capital attracted alongside its programs and £3.7 billion of lending supported through guarantees.

That financing benefited approximately 38,000 U.K. businesses, including around 30,000 businesses the Bank had not previously supported.

text:
VinFast Auto Ltd. (NASDAQ:VFS) has suspended plans to manufacture three electric vehicles in India and told suppliers to "hold all activities" on those programs while it reassesses costs, according to two sources and a company memo reviewed by Reuters.

The paused programs include the VF3, a two-door SUV expected to be VinFast's most competitive model in India, along with the VF6 and VF7 SUVs, which the company currently imports as kits from Vietnam and assembles locally. The move comes about a year after VinFast entered India, a market it turned to for growth after struggling to gain share in the U.S. VinFast told Reuters it plans to develop India-specific models rather than simply importing existing global ones, calling India an important part of its long-term strategy. The firm described the pause as a reasonable adjustment based on market research and consumer feedback.

Separately, VinFast said existing CKD assembly of the VF6 and VF7 at its Thoothukudi, Tamil Nadu plant continues unchanged; the pause applies specifically to deeper localization and development work.

Bull Case

VinFast Auto Ltd. (NASDAQ:VFS 's core delivery growth remains strong and continues to accelerate. Global EV deliveries reached 70,085 vehicles in the second quarter, up 96% year over year. The first-half deliveries rose 78% to 128,662. These figures show that the India localization pause has not stopped VinFast from increasing vehicle volumes across its other markets.

VinFast can use the break in India to spend its money more wisely. The company has pursued a more asset-light strategy. It includes plans to divest its Vietnam manufacturing entity. Its CFO has emphasized financial discipline and cost optimization. Hence, the firm can redirect capital toward markets and products that give stronger returns.

VinFast can also maintain its near-term India operations since the company says CKD assembly of the VF6 and VF7 continues at its Thoothukudi facility. It allows VinFast to keep serving Indian customers while it reassesses deeper localization for the VF3 and future models.

VinFast's two-wheeler business provides another significant growth opportunity. Electric scooter and e-bike deliveries jumped 311% year over year to 286,039 units in the second quarter. It gives VinFast a rapidly expanding business line beyond passenger EVs.

Bear Case

VinFast Auto Ltd. (NASDAQ:VFS) remains deeply unprofitable and continues to consume substantial amounts of cash. The company's trailing twelve-month net loss reached roughly $4.2 billion as of the first quarter, up about 33% year over year. VinFast also relies heavily on founder-backed funding, which could create extra financing and dilution risks for shareholders.

The India pause represents a setback to VinFast's expansion strategy. Reuters linked the decision to the company's broader struggle to gain market share in the U.S., while India represents another important market where VinFast had planned to expand its manufacturing footprint. Delaying deeper localization reduces one of the company's planned avenues for international growth.

The details surrounding the pause also raise concerns about cost pressures. The India manufacturing plans had not received public disclosure before the Reuters report, while a company memo reportedly asked suppliers to identify spending that could require payment or reimbursement. Those requests suggest that VinFast may have faced greater budget pressure than its public statements indicate.

VinFast also faces intense competition in India. Volkswagen and Nissan struggled to build significant market share in the country, while established players such as Suzuki, Hyundai and Tata already command strong customer loyalty and distribution networks. VinFast will need to invest heavily and execute effectively to establish an important position in the market.

NIO, the more established Asian EV exporter most often compared with VinFast, was held by 27 funds, down from 31, with holdings value falling to $371.7 million from $642.3 million.

Conclusion

VinFast Auto Ltd. (NASDAQ:VFS) keeps delivering strong volume growth, while its two-wheeler business and more disciplined capital strategy provide more avenues for expansion. However, the India manufacturing pause shows the company's cost pressures and execution challenges as it works with heavy losses and faces intense competition.

Overall, VinFast's quick delivery growth supports the bull case. However, investors need to see the company convert that growth into stronger financial results.

text:
The Philippines is moving to accelerate critical-mineral development across millions of hectares of land, raising concerns that expanded mining and faster permitting could put pressure on forests, ancestral domains, and Indigenous communities’ ability to give or withhold consent.

In an executive order signed on 18 August, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. established a national framework for developing the country’s critical-minerals industry. The order identifies at least 9 million hectares (22 million acres) of prospective areas that could host mineral resources, and calls for policies that promote downstream processing, investment, and “responsible and sustainable mining practices.”

Executive Order No. 122 directs the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), through its Mines and Geosciences Bureau, to implement a national exploration and mineral reservation program. It also orders mining applications to be streamlined through a virtual one-stop shop that will allow national and local permits and clearances to be processed simultaneously rather than sequentially.

The Legal Rights and Natural Resources Center (LRC), an environmental and Indigenous rights legal group, says the policy could expose a much larger area to mineral exploration and development.

“

Our survival as a species depends on a well-functioning ecosystem, nothing else. Listen to the local people and follow their advice when they express concerns and warnings regarding mining activities.

Rogelio Andrada II, director, Institute of Renewable Natural Resources University of the Philippines Los Baños

The 9-million-hectare figure represents about 30 per cent of the country’s land area, and is more than 11 times the 813,575 hectares (2.01 million acres) currently covered by approved mining projects, according to the LRC. EO 122, however, describes the 9 million hectares as prospective areas with potential mineral resources, rather than as approved mining projects.

Rogelio Andrada II, a forestry professor and director of the Institute of Renewable Natural Resources at the University of the Philippines Los Baños, said mineral exploration may be less disruptive but is not without impacts, while extraction can damage forests depending on the mineral, location, and technology used.

“Mining, whatever technology is used, is essentially disruptive to any ecosystem where it is done, whether forest, freshwater or grassland, because it is an extractive industry,” Andrada told Mongabay by email.

Pressure on ancestral lands

The LRC estimates that 424,830 hectares (1.05 million acres), or 54 per cent of the country’s existing approved mining area, potentially overlaps with ancestral domains.

Victor Colili, a Pala’wan Indigenous leader from Brooke’s Point on the island of Palawan, said further expansion would intensify pressures communities already experience. Colili’s community have for years opposed a nickel mining operation in their ancestral territory, which they say has damaged their environment.

“In Palawan, there is practically nowhere you can mine that is not forest and ancestral land,” Colili told Mongabay in a phone interview.

He added Indigenous families living within ancestral domains depend directly on forests and other natural resources for farming and subsistence.

“If their territory becomes smaller, the land they depend on for their daily livelihood also becomes smaller,” Colili said. “Their farms become smaller too, and that will lead to poverty.”

He also warned that mining can deepen divisions within Indigenous communities, particularly where royalty payments create competing interests over ancestral lands.

Faster permits raise consent concerns

LRC has also questioned EO 122’s simultaneous processing of permits and clearances, warning that the processes of obtaining affected communities’ free, prior, and informed consent, or FPIC, and public consultations could take place before communities have sufficient information about the impacts.

“Communities cannot give informed consent to a mining project if they have yet to see and understand the full environmental impacts of that project,” said LRC executive director E.M. Taqueban.

Colili raised a similar concern, saying communities need sufficient time to assess the potential impacts and complex agreements involved in mining projects before deciding whether to give their consent.

“If a decision is obtained through a process that is rushed, we Indigenous peoples could consider that a form of deception,” he said.

Mongabay sought comment from DENR through the agency’s press relations office, asking how it would ensure simultaneous permitting doesn’t weaken environmental assessment, public participation, or FPIC processes. The department had not responded by the time this story was published.

The mining industry, meanwhile, has welcomed streamlined permitting. The Philippine Nickel Industry Association called simultaneous rather than sequential processing “particularly encouraging,” saying its implementation should result in faster, clearer, and more predictable processes for investors.

Mining while protecting ecosystems

Andrada said mining remains necessary because some important minerals have no available alternatives, but extraction should preserve ecosystem health and ensure that economic benefits reach local communities.

“Our survival as a species depends on a well-functioning ecosystem, nothing else,” he said.

Where mining proceeds, Andrada said, some environmental impacts are inevitable, so safeguards should anticipate them and prevent irreversible ecosystem damage.

“Listen to the local people and follow their advice when they express concerns and warnings regarding mining activities,” he said, adding that local governments should prioritise the welfare of affected communities.

The Marcos administration says critical-mineral development should proceed alongside environmental protection and the social, cultural, and economic development of host communities. EO 122 also seeks to move the Philippines beyond raw extraction toward refining, manufacturing, and mineral recycling.

The LRC called on Congress to first pass the Alternative Minerals Management Bill, which seeks to reform mining policy by strengthening community participation and rights and incorporating ecosystem protection, before pursuing large-scale critical-mineral development.

The worldwide transition toward carbon neutrality and sustainable resource utilization has stimulated extensive research into advanced materials for renewable energy technologies. Among these materials, polymers have attracted particular attention because of their structural diversity, lightweight nature, solution-processability, and compatibility with scalable manufacturing methods. Continuous progress in molecular design, nanoscale engineering, and functional processing has enabled polymers to play increasingly important roles in energy harvesting, energy storage, electronic devices, and environmentally adaptive systems. As a result, polymer-based materials are now recognized as essential platforms for addressing modern challenges related to energy efficiency, environmental sustainability, and green technology development.

In recent years, substantial efforts have been directed toward the creation of multifunctional polymer systems that combine high performance with sustainable material concepts. Research activities involving recyclable polymers, degradable networks, bio-derived materials, and environmentally benign fabrication strategies have expanded rapidly in response to growing environmental concerns and circular-economy initiatives. Beyond traditional energy-related applications, polymer materials have also demonstrated considerable potential in flexible electronics, wearable devices, water treatment technologies, and environmentally responsive systems. These developments clearly demonstrate how polymer science continues to evolve into a highly interdisciplinary research field bridging chemistry, materials engineering, environmental science, and renewable energy technologies.

To showcase these rapidly advancing research directions, this Special Issue of Polymer Journal, entitled “Advanced Polymers in Renewable Energy Systems and Sustainability”, was organized to present recent achievements in sustainable polymer materials and energy-related technologies. The collected articles span a broad range of topics, including polymer photovoltaics, thermoelectric and ionic materials, recyclable and degradable polymers, bio-based systems, polymer electrolytes and membranes, multifunctional soft materials, wearable polymer devices, water purification technologies, and green processing methodologies.

This Special Issue was coordinated by Associate Editor Cheng-Liang Liu (Taiwan), together with Associate Editor Takuma Yasuda (Japan), Editor-in-Chief Keiji Tanaka (Japan), and Guest Editor Keun Hyung Lee (Korea). The editorial organization reflects the strong international collaboration within the Asian polymer community and highlights the interdisciplinary nature of sustainable polymer research. Through the efforts of the editorial team and the valuable contributions from leading researchers, this issue successfully collected 17 Original Articles, 3 Focus Reviews, 1 Review Article, and 1 Rapid Communication. These contributions present cutting-edge developments in sustainable polymer science and advanced energy-related materials, covering both fundamental investigations and practical applications. Several papers included in this issue investigate polymer systems for renewable energy conversion and advanced functional devices, including polymer solar cells, thermoelectric materials, ionic conductors, and hybrid composite systems. Other studies focus on sustainable polymer technologies involving recyclable networks, bio-derived materials, degradable polymers, and membrane-based environmental applications. In addition, contributions related to nanostructured polymers, self-assembled systems, and interfacial engineering further demonstrate how precise molecular and structural control can provide new opportunities for next-generation sustainable materials. We believe that this Special Issue will provide valuable perspectives for researchers working in polymer science, materials chemistry, renewable energy technologies, and sustainability-related disciplines. We also hope that the studies presented here will encourage further interdisciplinary collaborations and inspire future innovations in advanced polymer materials for sustainable energy and environmental applications. Finally, we would like to express our sincere appreciation to all authors for their excellent contributions and to all referees for their careful evaluation and constructive comments.

text:
Chesterfield County became a data center destination in Central Virginia with the arrival of three Google campuses, but a looming electricity shortfall is raising questions about whether the region’s power grid can keep up.

PJM Interconnection coordinates electricity distribution for 67 million people throughout 13 states (including Virginia) and Washington, D.C. — Dominion Energy, which serves Richmond, is one of the participating organizations.

Every year, PJM holds an auction in which energy providers, such as Dominion Energy, purchase commitments for the electricity capacity they’ll need to serve their customers at peak times three years from now.

Shannon Heckt is an energy and environment reporter for The Virginia Mercury and reports on PJM. She said when costs rise at auction, they are ultimately passed on to ratepayers through electricity bills.

“Dominion then has to buy that power at the capacity auction, and then if there's not enough power being generated, it leads to higher prices,” Heckt said. “It means Dominion has to pay more, which means that we all have to pay more.”

On July 14, this year’s PJM auction for the 2028/2029 distribution year (June 2028 to May 2029) fell short of PJM’s standard by nearly 6.8 gigawatts — enough to power at least 2.3 million homes and businesses.

So, why the deficit? PJM says the short answer is data centers.

“The results of the latest capacity auction show continuing trends of rapid large load growth driven by data centers, while generation is coming online at a much slower pace,” a PJM spokesperson wrote to The Richmonder.

Between 2024 and 2030, PJM predicts electricity demand will increase 32 gigawatts — 30 of which are from data centers “primarily in Virginia but also throughout the PJM footprint.”

PJM’s independent watchdog, Monitoring Analytics, said 38.2% of the market change was due to data centers, and recommended removing them from the auction entirely and making them buy power separately.

Other major power sucks — or as the industry calls them, “large loads” — include semiconductor plants and electricity-powered factories. Heckt said many of these are waiting for Dominion to offer them energy, so the company will likely have to build more power to meet demand.

“If they don’t start building more, whether it's gas plants or wind or solar, then there’s going to be more of a reliability crisis,” Heckt said.

Dominion is well aware of the issue. While it agrees data centers are a major component of increased demand, other major contributors are “the retirement of fossil-fuel, dispatchable generation resources and constraints on the transmission system,” a Dominion spokesperson wrote to The Richmonder.

Dominion says base rates are locked until its next biennial review in 2027, and PJM capacity costs will be a component. The auction’s impacts on customers’ bills won’t be known until this review. However, Dominion is confident data-center-driven costs won’t impact residential customers.

“We created a new rate class (GS-5) for high-energy customers, like data centers, as part of our 2025 biennial review and legislation from this year directs the SCC to assure during future biennial reviews that GS-5 customers are not being subsidized by other customers or otherwise causing adverse rate impacts,” Dominion’s emailed statement reads.

Demand for PJM’s resources reached an estimated all-time peak on July 2 at 168,158 megawatts — summer is typically when the most electricity is consumed throughout the year.

If nothing changes and demand increases faster than supply, this problem will likely compound. To curb the trend, PJM said it is using a price cap and floor for auctions until May 2030 to make sure consumers and suppliers don’t bear the brunt of increased costs.

“Reliability is PJM’s North Star. PJM is working on many fronts to rapidly and reliably integrate data centers and other so-called ‘large loads’ without impacting reliability to other customers,” PJM’s emailed statement reads. “Part of this includes constantly improving our forecasting for data center demand, because that information is used to procure generation capacity and plan for high voltage transmission.”

Heckt noted PJM also can kick large load data users — particularly data centers — off the electricity grid and onto backup generators. This option has usually entered the conversation during these super hot times of year. However, PJM has yet to do that.

This particularly affects Virginians. The commonwealth is home to the world’s highest concentration of data centers. Increased demand makes supply more expensive. Besides this, WMRA reported that expansions, repairs and replacements made to the electricity grid could also drive up costs for consumers.

“You just can’t take (data centers) out of the equation when we talk about why we need more power, because largely, in Virginia, it’s because of them,” Heckt said. “Obviously, there are more residents and there’s more electrification of things. Certainly that would increase things, but it’s going up by so much because of the data centers.”

These concerns are reflected in public opinion. A May Gallup poll found that cost-related worries are a major driver behind opposition to data centers, second only to these facilities’ environmental impact.

But development isn’t likely to slow down any time soon. In 2025, Google announced a $9 billion investment in Virginia to expand its cloud and artificial intelligence infrastructure, including three data center campuses planned for Chesterfield. Currently, the county’s Board of Supervisors isn’t interested in inviting more data centers.

Gov. Abigail Spanberger has defended the commonwealth’s commitment to making itself attractive to data center development. In an interview with Politico, Spanberger said data centers have long been a part of Virginia’s economy and support public goods such as schools, libraries and fire stations.

Spanberger also noted that data centers will be constructed one way or another. She argued that if Virginia turned away the industry, it would lose the chance to help set the standard for how data centers are built and operated, including environmental safeguards and technological investments.

“If we were to end that in one fell swoop, that has a major impact on jobs in Virginia, union jobs, electrical jobs, certainly the building trades,” Spanberger told Politico. “It has a major impact on many of our communities.”

Currently, the average wait time to become connected to Dominion’s grid is as many as seven years, Heckt said. What that means for data centers — like the ones setting up shop in Chesterfield — is that they’re securing their permits and starting construction while waiting in the wings.

“What you’re seeing in Chesterfield with these other data centers is that they’re going through the process,” Heckt said. “Obviously they won’t be able to be connected until much later, unless they decide to do behind-the-meter power, where they build their own power — usually gas turbines on site to power themselves — which supposedly shortens that time. But it still takes years to get that kind of infrastructure up.”

As for Dominion, the company says it’s planning for increased demand. The spokesperson said Dominion is looking to keep “building the infrastructure that is needed and at the pace that’s required” to continue meeting customers’ needs.

The Richmonder contacted Google for comment, but didn’t receive a response before publication.

text:
People across Wales are being invited to have their say on proposals for a new public energy company owned by the people of Wales.

A consultation launched today, sets out proposals for a single national public energy company. The company would bring together existing energy organisations and help ensure that more of the economic benefits from Wales’s energy resources flow to people, communities, businesses and public services in Wales.

Wales has some of the best renewable energy resources in Europe. The proposed company would aim to increase Welsh ownership of energy projects and help communities, businesses and public services make better use of energy produced in Wales.

The company would not replace existing energy suppliers or directly set household energy prices. However, increasing Welsh ownership of energy projects could help reduce energy costs over time and ensure more money is reinvested in Welsh communities and public services.

Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy, Adam Price, said:

“Wales has huge potential to generate clean energy from our natural resources.

“We want to make sure the benefits of that energy are felt by people and communities across Wales, both in jobs and growth but eventually in lower bills too.

“Wales is on the verge of a second (or another) energy revolution and this time we want to make sure we keep more of the benefits here.

This consultation is about how we can build a stronger Welsh energy sector, support local ownership and create lasting value for future generations. It’s about cheaper, cleaner energy that is made and owned in Wales.

“We want to hear from people, communities, businesses and organisations across Wales about how this company should work and what it should deliver.”

While the proposals laid out in this consultation aim to cut energy bills in the future, the Welsh Government is using every tool available to them to help households cope with their energy bills. This year we are investing more than £37m in our Nest scheme to help low-income families escape cold, damp conditions, and continue to invest in direct support through fuel vouchers and heating assistance.

The Claim What’s Yours service helps people check their eligibility for extra income and guide them through the claiming process. For free, confidential, advice, call 0800 702 2020.
